**can study all manner of fine arts and languages quickly and nimbly, without**

<meta>This page continues the preface of the polemical work introduced on the previous page. The author is establishing a theological foundation by comparing the soul of a believer to a rose, a metaphor likely chosen to contrast with the "Rosicrucian" (Rose Cross) movement he intends to criticize.</meta>

# Preface.

<meta>catchword: Dar- (The beginning of the word "Darzu," meaning "thereto," continuing from the previous page's final sentence.)</meta>

...to the daughters. For just as a little rose is a lovely and laudable creature and a hearty creation of God—which delights, cools, strengthens, and refreshes humanity through its beautiful form, pleasant scent, and special operation and effect, as the natural philosophers and physicians <note>original Latin: "Physici & Medici"</note> write regarding it: <note>The author cites classical and Renaissance authorities: Dioscorides, Book 1, Chapter 13; Galen, Book 8, "On the Power of Simple Medicines"; Pliny, Book 21, Chapter 4; Serapion the Younger; and Leonhart Fuchs.</note> It is likewise the same with pious Christians in this valley of tears <note>original: "Jammerthal"; a common Baroque expression for the earthly world of suffering</note>, as David calls it in Psalm 84. Since God the LORD has created and made us into the people and the sheep of His heath and pasture (Psalms 95 and 100), that we should be His own, serving Him in holiness and righteousness that is pleasing to Him (Luke 1). He Himself has planted us, so that we should be trees of righteousness and seedlings of the Lord for His praise (Isaiah 61). He has ransomed <note>original: "ranzionirt," from the French "rançonner"</note> and redeemed us at a very great price (1 Corinthians 6), not with perishable gold or silver, but with His own precious blood and with His innocent suffering and death (1 Peter 1). Thus, with special honor and renown, we may well be titled and named the most hearty creatures and the noblest of God's creations, because the LORD has His highest and greatest delight in us, the children of men (Proverbs 8).

He loves us so fervently that His love is stronger than death, which many waters cannot quench nor the floods drown (Song of Solomon 8). For He did not spare His only Son (Romans 8), even when we were yet His enemies (Romans 5), but gave Him up for our sins (Romans 4)—and not only for ours, but for the sins of the whole world (1 John 2). This was so that all who believe in Him and persevere steadfastly in faith should not be lost, but have eternal life (John 3, Matthew 10). We should forever use this for our true heart's refreshment <note>original: "herzlabung"</note> and, out of a wonder born of strong faith, say with Moses: how the LORD loves the people so much; all His saints are in His hand; they shall sit at His feet and shall learn from His words (Deuteronomy 33). Taste and see how friendly the LORD is (Psalm 39 <note>In the German Bible of the time, this is often Psalm 34</note>); His mercy is as great as He Himself is (Sirach 18), and His love is so fervent that He cannot act according to His righteous anger (Hosea 11). Just as a father has mercy on his children, so the LORD has mercy on those who fear Him (Psalm 103).

<summary>The author uses a complex floral metaphor to argue that true Christians are God's "roses," redeemed by Christ's blood, contrasting this biblical dignity with the "errors" of the groups he opposes.</summary>
<keywords>Rose metaphor, Creation, Redemption, Valley of Tears, Divine Love, Classical Medicine, Biblical Citations</keywords>

# Preface.

<sig>A iij</sig>
<meta>catchword: holy (The German catchword "heiliger" anticipates the first word of the next page, likely "Geiliget" or "sanctified.")</meta>

Thereafter, just as a rose has two distinct colors—red and white—in the same way every pious Christian must possess these same colors: *not according to external splendor, but according to internal beauty* <note>original Latin: "non secundum splendorem externum, sed secundum decorem internum"</note>. He must be Red—that is, sprinkled with the precious, rose-colored blood of Jesus Christ, which occurs in the holy sacraments and in the healing sermons of the Gospel; which St. Peter therefore calls the **sprinkling of the blood** <note>original Greek: "ῥαντισμὸν τοῦ αἵματος"</note> of Jesus Christ, 1 Peter 1. For when a preacher teaches and preaches of Christ and His grace-filled merit, he does nothing else—just as in the administration and distribution of the sacraments—than sprinkle his listeners, the baptismal candidates, and the communicants with the holy, precious, rose-colored blood of Jesus Christ. And in the highly venerable Lord’s Supper, by the power of the sun-clear words of the Testament, he truly gives them to drink and refreshes them by means of the blessed wine, as the man of God, Luther, quite gloriously and beautifully writes concerning this in Volume 7 of the Jena edition, folio 405. The preacher's tongue, he says, is the **sprinkling brush** <note>original: "Sprengwedel," referring to an aspergillum or hyssop used for sprinkling holy water; here used metaphorically for the distribution of Christ's blood through the Word.</note>; he dips it into the rose-colored blood of the Lord Christ and sprinkles the people with it. That is, he preaches the Gospel to them, which declares that Christ has obtained forgiveness of sins through His precious blood, which He shed on the Cross for the sins of the whole world. Whoever believes this is sprinkled therewith, and hears the gracious voice of comfort of the Lord saying to him: "Though your sins be as blood-red, they shall be made as white as snow; and though they be like rose-color <note>original: "Rosinfarbe," often used in this period to denote crimson or scarlet in biblical translations</note>, they shall become like wool," Isaiah 1. For I am the LORD your God, the Holy One of Israel, your Savior; I, even I, blot out your transgressions for my own sake, and will not remember your sins, Isaiah 43.

Furthermore, a Christian must also be White, inside and out—that is, lead a holy, pure, and fine life, letting the light of faith shine (Matthew 5) and serving God in holiness and righteousness that is pleasing to Him (Luke 1), according to the ability He grants. *For faith works through love in the heart, even if it does not always manifest outwardly in works* <note>original Latin: "fides enim per dilectionem operatur in corde, etsi foris non semper exit in opere." The author attributes this to Sedulius Scotus, a 9th-century Irish teacher, in his commentary on Romans 3.</note>. For to this end we were created by GOD the Father, redeemed by GOD the Son, and by GOD the Holy Spirit sanc-

# Preface.

<meta>catchword: themselves (The original catchword "ipsi" refers to the first word of the next page in the Latin phrase "ut ipsi.")</meta>

...sanctified / so that we should not let sin reign in our mortal bodies / to obey it in its lusts / but that we should surrender ourselves to God / Romans 6. And as He is holy / so that we also are holy / Lev. 19. 1 Pet. 1. Since we have died to the regulations of the world / Col. 2. and risen with Christ / therefore we must also walk in a new life / Rom. 6. and strive for what is above / and not for what is on Earth / Col. 3. We should love God heartily / and thank Him for all His benefits / and say with David / "Bless now the Lord, my soul, and forget not what good He has done for you" / Ps. 103. For God is love / and whoever remains in love / remains in God / and God in him / through this, love is perfected in us / so that we may have a joyfulness on the Day of Judgment / 1 John 4. However, we must also not forget the love of neighbor / for that is the foremost and greatest commandment / "You shall love God the Lord with all your heart / with all your soul / and with all your mind" / the other, however, is like it / "You shall love your neighbor as yourself" / Matth. 22.

Thirdly / just as a beautiful and lovely little rose is among the stinging thorns / by which it must let itself be pricked and broken / and nonetheless grows up quite elegantly and heartily / flourishes, turns green, and blooms / even though some of the ancient Church Fathers consider / that before the Fall, roses did not come up among and with the thorns / but the thorns first sprouted after the curse / which was laid upon the earth because of sin / Gen. 3. alongside the roses / Basil, homily 5 on the *Hexaemeron* <note>The *Hexaemeron* refers to theological treatises on the six days of creation described in Genesis.</note>. Ambrose, book 3 of the *Hexaemeron*, chapters 9 & 11. Alcuin, book 3, chapter 18. Augustine, however, having changed his earlier opinion which he held in book 1 of *Against the Manicheans on Genesis*, chapter 13, now thinks that thorns grew alongside roses from their very first origin / book 3 of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 18 & book 83 <note>original Latin: "Augustinus autem priori sententia mutata quam habet lib. 1. de Genes. cont. Manich. c. 13. existimat rosis mox à prima origine adnatas fuisse spinas, lib 3. de Genes. ad lit. c. 18. & lib. 83."</note>. This is exactly how it is with pious Christians on Earth / they must let themselves be pricked and broken, pushed and forced / by the stinging thorns of this world in the most poisonous and violent way: Not indeed when they are paternally disciplined by God / but when the world hates and envies them: For the tribulations and paternal discipline of God are good for us / so that we may be tested and exercised by them / for the saints are tested for this reason, so that they themselves <note>original Latin: "ideo enim tentantur sancti, ut ipsi"</note>

# Preface.

<meta>catchword: ders (this catchword refers to the beginning of the word "derselbigen" or "derselben" on the following page)</meta>

...so that they may recognize themselves, <note>original: "ipsi se agnoscent"</note> as Primasius says on 2 Corinthians 1, or as Jerome says in Book 6 of his *Commentary on Isaiah*: "God strikes so that He may improve." <note>original: "Deus percutit ut emendet"</note> But the **scoundrel’s luck** <term>Bubenglück: a derogatory term for the undeserved prosperity of the wicked</term> of the godless grieves us greatly when we are envied and persecuted by them; yet we should not let such "heat of temptation" <note>original: "hitze der anfechtung"</note> alienate us, *1 Peter 4.* For it is thus decreed that all who wish to live godly lives in Christ Jesus must suffer persecution, *2 Timothy 3,* and we must enter the Kingdom of God through much cross-bearing and tribulation, *Acts 14.*

Wherefore Solon rightly says in Herodotus, page 2: "Man is entirely a misfortune" <note>original: "πᾶν ἐστ’ ἄνθρωπος συμφορὴ homo totum quod est, obnoxium est calamitatibus"</note>; man is subject to all kinds of misery and wretchedness. And if the Lord were not with us when men set themselves against us, they would swallow us alive; when their anger rages against us, the waters would drown us, streams would go over our soul, the waters would go far too high over our soul, *Psalm 124.* In this same way, man is called **Enosh** <note>original: אֱנֹושׁ</note> in Hebrew because he must dwell here in misery and walk through the valley of sorrows. The word "human" <note>original: "Mensch"</note> also aims at and reflects this: as if one said "man of ash." <note>The author is using a folk etymology, linking the German word "Mensch" to "Man" and "Asche" (ash), suggesting human frailty.</note> In this fashion, the Patriarchs of the Old Testament gave names to their children by which they remembered their state of distress; as Moses named his first son **Gershom**, *Exodus 2,* from the root meaning "to be a stranger," <note>original: גֵּרְשֹׁום (gershom) / "peregrinari"</note> because he had been a stranger in a foreign land. And the word **German** <note>Germanus</note> also has its origin and beginning from "stranger" and "wretched." <note>original: גֵּרִים (gerim) and עֲנִי (ani), "hoc est, advenæ miseri." The author is claiming the word "German" comes from Hebrew roots meaning "miserable strangers."</note>

For the Patriarchs and Prophets were certainly plagued people, and the Apostles also had to experience all kinds of need and death, and **confirm** and seal their confession of Christ Jesus with their own blood. Oh, how unmercifully they were often torn apart and scourged, and martyred and butchered in the most gruesome ways! As the Church Histories state and show, the persecution did not end with them but has landed upon us as well, and lasts forever and ever until the beloved Last Day. Thus, Bernard <note>Saint Bernard of Clairvaux</note> in his *Book of Meditations* may well lament and say: "Man is nothing other than foul seed, a juice of dung, food for worms; after man, a worm; after the worm, stench and horror." <note>original: "homo nihil aliud est quàm sperma fœtidum, succus stercorum, cibus vermium, post hominem vermis, post vermem fætor & horror"</note> We are nothing else...

<meta>This page continues the preface's discussion on the nature of human suffering. # Preface.

<note>The text continues from the previous page: "...nothing other than..."</note> than stinking earthworms, subjected to all kinds of distress and finally to death.

For only consider how horribly and inhumanly the bloodthirsty and tyrannical Emperors have raged and acted as tyrants against the Christian Church: Nero, Domitian, Trajan, Marcus Antoninus, Severus, Maximinus, Decius, Valerian, Aurelian, and Diocletian. These men did not merely cause a localized flood of water, but a horrific deluge <note>original: "Sündflut," referring to the Great Flood of Noah</note> of blood throughout the Empire, and within thirty days caused some 17,000 Christians to be mercilessly executed for the sake of their Christian faith. Consider also Julian the Apostate, Valens, and similar tyrants, of whom the histories of the Church and others write sufficiently. *Augustine, Book 18 of The City of God, chapter 52; Eusebius, Book 3 of Ecclesiastical History, chapters 15, 17, 30, and Book 4, chapter 2, and Book 1 of the Life of Constantine.* What shall or can we say in complaint against the Pope? How many hundreds of thousands might he have had killed from the year 1517 <note>The year Martin Luther posted his 95 Theses, signaling the start of the Reformation</note> until these current times for the sake of the faith and the Lutheran religion? For this is the singular bloodthirsty tone of their speech: "Wipe them out, wipe them out with the Lutherans! To the fire with such heretics!" *Gregory de Valentia, Volume 3, dispute 1, question 11, punishment 2; Louis d’Orléans, part 29; Reinaldus in his Rosary, page 157; Jacobus Simancha, Catholic Institutes, chapter 46, number 52; Stanislaus Cristanovitz in his Examination of the Catholic English Edict; Conradus Brunus on Heretics, book 3, chapter 15; Paulus Chirlandus on Heretics, question 3, number 2.* Thus they also frequently hold bloodthirsty councils, debating whether it would be better to craftily exterminate the Evangelicals <note>Protestants</note> with the sword, muskets, gunpowder, or with poison. And whoever perpetrates such murder and tyranny is canonized by the Pope—that "pious" child, <note>The author is being deeply sarcastic here.</note> <insert>namely the son of perdition, 2 Thessalonians 2</insert> and is numbered among the saints. *See Bellarmine on the Roman Pontiff, book 5, chapter 7; Becanus, volume 1, page 400; Brunus on Heretics, book 3, last chapter, page 309; Juan de Mariana, Jesuit of Toledo, on the King, book 1, chapter 7, pages 65 and 67.*

Because all pious Christians, like a beautiful little rose, must allow themselves to be pricked and broken by the sharp thorns of this world, and remain subject to all kinds of misery and distress, they certainly will not be able to live here in joy. Rather, the closer the end of the world approaches, the more the Devil will rage and storm, just as Daniel prophesied that it shall be such a sorrowful time, as

<meta>This page continues the preface's discussion of religious persecution. The previous page cataloged the cruelties of Roman Emperors and the Papacy against the Church. This page concludes that thought by referencing the biblical prophecy of the Devil's "short time" of wrath before pivoting to a message of comfort for the faithful, contrasting the temporary suffering of the godly with the eventual downfall of the wicked.</meta>

# Preface.

A iiij

...the likes of which has not been heard before, since people have existed (Daniel, Chapter 12). And the Evangelical <term>Seer</term> <note>original: "Vident," a Latinate term for a visionary or prophet</note> John laments and says (Revelation 12): "Woe to those who dwell on earth, for the devil has come down to you, and has a great wrath, and knows that he has little time."

Even though the devil rages and tyrannizes so fiercely during this short time in which he is set loose (Revelation 20), he can nevertheless do us no harm, neither to body nor soul, without God's <term>indulgence</term> <note>original: "indulgentz," here meaning divine permission or allowance</note> and decree, as can be seen from the history of Job (Chapters 1 and 2). Much less can he separate us from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus our Lord (Romans 8). Therefore, we do not fear his cunning and power, nor any of his henchmen, in the slightest. Rather, we say with the ancient Church Father Ambrose (Volume 5, folio 215): <note>original Latin: "Væ illis quibus diabolus amicus est, nam quamto amplius est cuilibet amicus, tamto ampliora ei tormenta ingerit, infelix est enim amicitia diaboli"</note> "Woe to those to whom the devil is a friend; for the more he is a friend to anyone, the greater the torments he heaps upon them, for the friendship of the devil is a miserable thing."

For although the devil's enemies must pass through the <term>Vale of Tears</term> <note>original: "Jammerthal," a common metaphor for the hardships and sorrows of earthly life</note> here and eat bitter gall and the <note>original Latin: "panem doloris"</note> "bread of sorrow," it is nevertheless only a <note>original Latin: "parva nubecula"</note> "little cloud," or a <note>original Latin: "modicum"</note> "brief moment" (John 16). And the Lord Christ saves the good wine for them at last (John 2) and makes them drink deeply of the rich goods of His house (Psalm 36). He crowns them with grace as with a shield (Psalm 5) and showers them with eternal joy that cannot be taken from them (John 16). 

The devil's friends, however, may flourish here in this world like a laurel tree, and they are not in misfortune like other folk, nor are they plagued like other men (Psalm 73). But they cannot remain in such dignity; instead, they must depart like cattle, and their deeds are pure folly. They lie in hell like sheep, and death gnaws upon them (Psalm 49).

Therefore, it is better to be God's friend and the devil's enemy, despite all hardship and persecution. For it cannot be otherwise: whoever wishes to live a godly life must enter the Kingdom of God through much <term>cross-bearing</term> <note>original: "Creuz," literally "cross," referring to the trials and burdens of a Christian</note> and tribulation (Acts 14). As Sirach also says (Chapter 2): "My child, if you wish to be God's servant, then prepare yourself for temptation." We shall be well rewarded in heaven, as Paul indicates: the suffering of this present time is not worthy of the glory that shall be revealed in us (Romans 8).

# Preface.

...rather than stinking earthworms, subjected to all kinds of misery and finally to death.

For consider how horribly and inhumanely the bloodthirsty and tyrannical emperors raged and tyrannized against the Christian Church: Nero, Domitian, Trajan, Marcus Antoninus, Severus, Maximinus, Decius, Valerian, Aurelian, and Diocletian. (The latter did not merely cause a flood of water, but a horrific <term>deluge of sin</term> <note>original: "Sündflut," typically referring to the Great Flood of Noah, used here to describe the overwhelming scale of the persecution</note> in the Empire, and within thirty days had some 17,000 Christians mercilessly executed for the sake of their Christian faith). Julian, Valens, and similar tyrants also raged, of whom the Church histories and other chronicles write sufficiently: Augustine, *The City of God*, Book 18, Chapter 52; Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 3, Chapters 15, 17, and 30; Book 4, Chapter 2; and Book 1, *The Life of Constantine*. 

What should or can we say and lament regarding the Pope? How many hundred thousands might he have had killed from the year 1517 until these present times for the sake of the faith and the Lutheran religion? For this is their singular, bloodthirsty <term>tune</term>: <note>original: "Zungenthon," literally "tongue-tone" or "refrain"</note> "Away with them, away with them with the Lutherans! To the fire with such heretics!" (Gregory de Valentia, Volume 3, dispute 1, question 11; Louis d’Orléans, part 29; Reinald in his *Rosary*, page 157; Jacob Simancha, *Catholic Institutes*, Chapter 46; Stanislaus Cristanovic in his *Examination of the Catholic English Edict*; Conrad Brun, *On Heretics*, Book 3, Chapter 15; Paolo Grillando, *On Heretics*, question 3). 

They also frequently hold bloodthirsty councils to determine whether it is better to cunningly exterminate the Evangelicals with the sword, muskets, powder, or with poison. And whoever carries out such a murder and tyranny, the Pope—that "pious child," <term>namely of perdition</term> <note>original Latin: "scilicet perditionis," a reference to the Antichrist in 2 Thessalonians 2:3</note>—canonizes him and counts him among the saints (see Bellarmine, *On the Roman Pontiff*, Book 5, Chapter 7; Becan, Volume 1, page 400; Brun, *On Heretics*, Book 3, last chapter, page 309; Juan de Mariana, Jesuit of Toledo, *On the King*, Book 1, Chapter 7, pages 65 and 67).

Since all pious Christians, like a beautiful little rose, must allow themselves to be pricked and broken by the prickly thorns of this world, and remain subject to all kinds of misery and distress, they certainly will not be able to live in joy here. Rather, the closer the end of the world comes, the more the devil will rage and storm, just as the prophet Daniel foretold: that it shall be such a sorrowful time as...

Although it is certain from God’s Word, and known and recognized from daily and lamentable experience, that the Cross and tribulation are the courtly livery and hallmark of all true little children of God in the Kingdom of Christ—wherefore David also calls the life of pious Christians <term>עמק הבכא</term> <gloss>Emek Ha-Bakha</gloss>, a <term>Vale of Tears</term> <note>Psalm 84:6; a biblical metaphor for the suffering of earthly life</note>—nevertheless, not only did the <term>Chiliasts</term> <note>From the Greek word for "thousand," referring to those who believe in a literal 1,000-year earthly reign of Christ</note> or <term>Millenarians</term> of old, such as Nepos, Cerinthus, and their like, rise up against this and dream of a Jewish paradise <note>as witnessed by the ancient historians Eusebius in *Church History*, Book 7, Chapter 22, and Nicephorus, Book 3, Chapter 14</note>; but now, the "new Chiliasts" and enthusiasts—<term>Nagelius</term>, <term>Felgenhauer</term>, and <term>Hartprecht</term> <note>Paul Nagel, Paul Felgenhauer, and Johann Hartprecht were controversial 17th-century thinkers who predicted an imminent golden age on earth</note>—declare themselves anew. They seek to transform the Christians' Vale of Tears, contrary to God’s word and will, into a Hall of Joy, and they dream of such a fleshly kingdom in which Christ shall live here on Earth for 1,000 years with His fellow subjects in all manner of luxury, showering His believers with magnificent eating and drinking, and forcing and bringing all their enemies under their feet.

But such heresy—to say nothing of other paradoxes and loathsome errors which are being spread by them throughout precious Christendom, as can be seen from this book—is very dangerous and harmful. It eats away like gangrene <note>literally "cancer disease"; 2 Timothy 2:17</note> and creeps up on many people, cunningly taking them in; for everyone would gladly want to be a great lord in the world and live in bridal joy and luxury. Therefore, it is not unnecessary that the simple-minded be warned, so that everyone might guard and provide for themselves against such deception with the greatest possible diligence, just as the Lord Christ Himself commanded us to <term>προσέχειν</term> <gloss>prosechein</gloss> <note>original Greek: "to take heed" or "beware"; Matthew 7:15</note>, and to remain with God’s Word in all humility and Christian simplicity, giving it the audience and reverence it is due. For the way of these new Chiliasts is like a slippery path in the dark, upon which they slide and fall, as Jeremiah says in Chapter 23. Their words are sweet like honey in the mouth, but afterward they become like wormwood and gall <note>literally "gentian," a bitter herb</note> and cause a cramping in the belly (Revelation 10). They may well say: "The Lord has revealed it to us, and the Spirit of God has proclaimed it to us; things will go happily and well for the believers in the 1,000 years." But who has stood in the counsel of the Lord, that he should see His word? Who has perceived and heard His word? For everything that is not revealed in God’s word—

I have, however, wished to assign this book by dedicating <note>original Latin: *dedicando*</note> it to **Your Noble Lordships**, not only because you harbor a heartfelt desire and love for God’s pure and unadulterated word, but also because you help to promote it as much as possible. For this reason, I also most faithfully recommend and commend you to Divine protection, and myself to the favor and promotion of **Your Noble Lordships**. # A Brief Summary of this Hero-Book of the Rose Garden / what is taught in each chapter / as well as which questions are discussed and dealt with therein.

In the <term>prolegomena</term> <note>original: *Prolegomenis*; an introductory section or preface</note>, or at the entrance and beginning of this book, it is shown that these new <term>Millenarians</term> <note>original: *Chiliasten*; those who believe in a literal thousand-year reign of Christ on Earth before the final judgment</note> and dreamers are not unjustly assigned and referred to the number of <term>heretics</term> <note>original: *Ketzer*</note>. Thereafter, these questions are treated and discussed:
1. Why they are called new prophets.
2. Why they are called brothers of the <term>Rosy Cross</term> <note>original: *RosenCreutz*; referring to the Rosicrucians, a mysterious spiritual and cultural movement that arose in Europe in the early 17th century</note>.
3. Why they are called Millenarians.
4. Why they are called <term>Enthusiasts</term> <note>original: *Enthusiasten*; in this period, a derogatory term for those who claimed to receive direct, private revelations from God</note>.

## The First Chapter.

Whether it is useful, beneficial, and necessary to send the youth to school, and how one should learn the <term>liberal arts</term> <note>original: *gute Künste*; referring to the traditional academic disciplines like grammar and logic</note> and languages from youth onward: Therein the following questions are handled and discussed.
1. Whether it is necessary that schools be established and maintained, and the youth sent there to learn something?
2. What reasons these new Enthusiasts and "heavenly prophets" have for despising and rejecting primary schools and universities <note>original: *die kleinen und hohen Schulen*; literally "the small and high schools"</note>.
3. Whether all liberal arts and languages are not hidden within us.
4. How the new Enthusiasts prove that all arts lie hidden by nature within man.
5. Whether one can become learned through prayer alone?
6. Whether one can become learned without books?
7. Since, according to the statement of the new Enthusiasts, no books are needed for study, it is further asked: whether someone can also attain skill and proficiency without effort and labor?
8. How soon then might someone become learned?
9. Whether the <term>learner</term> <note>original Latin: *disens*</note>, or the one who is learning, becomes essentially one with that which he learns?
10. Whether it is also necessary to learn languages and the liberal arts?
11. Whether it is necessary to study <term>Grammar, Logic, and Rhetoric</term> <note>original: *Grammaticam, Dialecticam vnd Rhetoricam*; the "Trivium," which formed the foundation of a classical education</note> from youth onward?
12. Should one also read pagan books?

## The Fourth Chapter.

What the new Millenarians / but especially <term>Weigel</term> <note>Valentin Weigel (1533–1588), a German pastor and mystic whose radical ideas on internal spirituality were published after his death and caused great controversy</note> hold and believe regarding God / the Fall of the first man / free will / sin / the Sacrament of Holy Baptism / and the venerable Lord's Supper / and other Articles of Faith / specifically, these questions are treated and handled therein.

1. What Weigel teaches and believes concerning the Article of the Holy Trinity?
2. What the state of man was before the Fall / whether it was necessary for him to be both good and evil at the same time?

# Thorough Account of the New Prophets, Rosicrucians, Chiliasts, and Enthusiasts.

What heresy and human doctrine actually are, the seer <term>Zechariah</term> <note>Referring to the biblical prophet Zechariah, specifically chapter 5, verse 3</note> presents and sets before us as a fine image and masterly painting in the **flying book** <note>original: *fliegenden Buche*; in modern biblical translations of Zechariah 5:1, this is usually rendered as a "flying scroll"</note> which the Prophet saw when he lifted up his eyes. For through this book nothing else is **prefigured** <note>original: *praefigurirt*</note> and depicted but art, wisdom, and skill, inasmuch as books are also the **identifying marks** <note>original: γνωρίσματα</note> of the learned—but not the divine wisdom, nor the true theological art and understanding, which is taken from Scripture and deeply rooted and grounded in God’s Word. What heresy and human doctrine actually are is presented and held before us as a fine image and masterly painting by the spirit-enlightened <term>Seer Zechariah</term> <note>original: *Vident Zacharias*; referring to the Old Testament prophet</note> in Chapter 5, verse 3, in the flying scroll <note>original: *fliegenden Buche*</note> which the prophet saw when he had opened his eyes. # From the Rose Garden.

<margin>Folio 961.</margin> Thus we read in *Georgius Nicolai’s Collection of Histories, Book 24*, that in the year of Christ 1589, a nobleman from Silesia named Melchior von Langenau arrived in Dresden on June 28th. He was dressed in a long white robe which, like his hat, was decorated in front with small black crosses and cinched with yellow buckram bands. He called himself **Elias** and brought with him a book of 700 pages of various colors, in which the Catechism and other sayings were written, and he had drawn scissors throughout it. He titled this his "letter," and it was twenty cubits long and ten cubits wide <note>A cubit (German: *Elle*) was a traditional unit of measurement based on the length of the forearm. The enormous dimensions of the book are meant to mirror the "flying scroll" of Zechariah 5:2.</note>. Now, although his intent and purpose—which was to warn His Electoral Grace against **Calvinism** <note>A branch of Protestantism following John Calvin. In 1589, Saxony was embroiled in fierce theological disputes between "Gnesio-Lutherans" and "Crypto-Calvinists."</note>—is not to be <term>disapproved</term> <note>original: *improbiren*</note>, yet his method of persuasion and dissuasion <note>original: *modus suadendi & dissuadendi*</note> is not to be <term>approved</term> <note>original: *adprobiren*</note>. For it seems not unlike the flying book of **Zechariah**, seeing as the LORD God has given us the Law and the Testimony, and we should direct ourselves according to those, as seen in *Isaiah 8*. As **St. Peter** also says in his second epistle, chapter 1: "We have a firm prophetic word, and you do well to pay attention to it as to a light that shines in a dark place, until the day breaks and the morning star rises in your hearts."

> We are not permitted to indulge in anything of our own choosing, nor to choose what someone else has introduced of their own will. We have the Apostles of the Lord as our authorities, who did not choose to introduce anything of their own will, but faithfully assigned to the nations the teaching they received from Christ. <note>original Latin: *Nobis nihil ex nostro arbitrio indulgere licet, sed nec eligere, quod aliquis de arbitrio suo induxerit : Apostolos Domini habemus autores, qui nec ipsi quicquam ex suo arbitrio, quod inducerent, elegerunt, sed acceptam à Christo disciplinam fideliter nationibus assignaverunt*</note> Tertullian, *On the Prescription Against Heretics*.
> 
> For it is a ridiculous thing for one who presumes to speak with others from the prophetic writings to then disregard those very writings, and not always cite the same scriptures, but to think that he himself can find and speak something better than the holy scriptures. <note>original Latin: *Ridicula enim res est, eum qui ex propheticis literis cum alijs colloquendo verba facere præsumit eas literas posthabere, & non easdem scripturas semper allegare, sed seipsum melius quidquam, quàm sanctas literas invenire & eloqui posse existimare*</note> Justin Martyr, *Dialogue with Trypho the Jew*.

# Concerning the Rose Garden.

just as a book has many different leaves and sheets, so too are they a whole guild and sworn gang—as they call themselves, the **Brothers of the Rose Cross** <note>original: "Fratres Roseæ crucis"</note>, the anointed brothers of the **Rosy Cross**. # About the Rose Garden.
i.
<meta>catchword: you will</meta>

The Holy Luther compares the false spirits to the thistles which stand in the grain, Volume 8, folio 303. The sectarian spirits <term>Rottengeister</term> <note>original: "Rottengeister." A term frequently used by Luther to describe radical reformers or "factions" who broke away from his mainstream Reformation.</note>, he says, have an appearance among the people like the beautiful, large thistles that stand among the grain, with their brown heads, which grow higher and have a more magnificent appearance than the grain. They have fine green leaves, beautiful, wide, and brown heads; they bloom and glow there like a beautiful harlot <note>original: "Metze." In this period, it could mean a common girl or, more likely in this polemic context, a prostitute/harlot, emphasizing a deceptive, superficial beauty.</note>; they are red, beautiful, and strong. In contrast, the dear grain has no beautiful or magnificent form, but stands in the field quite pale-yellow. Anyone who does not know both would surely swear an oath—because the thistles stand in the good soil and in the middle of the grain, making themselves so thick and wide that they often suppress the grain—that they must be very good, useful flowers and herbs. But they are only evil, prickly thistles, useful to no one, indeed almost harmful; wherever one touches them, they prick one’s hands. Thistles they are and thistles they remain, and there is nothing in them to be improved until the reaper comes over them, cuts them down, and throws them into the fire, or makes a wreath for the Devil out of them.

So also do the **New Chiliasts** <note>Those who believe in a literal thousand-year reign of Christ on earth.</note>; they flourish and turn green in their imagined wisdom like a thorn bush, so that many a person would think everything they teach and write were right and good. And for this, they still wish to be beyond reproach; *they have a mouth which, lacking a door, is not shut* <note>original Latin: "os habent quod porta carens non clauditur."</note>—as Chrysostom says in his sermon on heretics—daring to prick and break, like thorns and thistles, those who oppose and rebel against them. In this manner, **Paulus Felgenhauer** <note>A controversial 17th-century German visionary and writer who claimed special divine inspiration.</note> clearly writes in the *Mirror of the Times* <note>original: "ZeitSpiegel."</note> at letter F. ij.: "He who is not higher in the Spirit than I am, let him leave me in peace; for I am called *touch me not* <note>original Latin: "noli me tangere."</note>, otherwise [you will]..."

A false spirit has gone out and produces and testifies itself actively in their mouths (1 Kings 22), and the Lord has not sent them, nor poured out the Spirit of wisdom and truth over them, that he might rule and lead them on a level path (Psalm 143). For whoever says anything <unclear>contrary to the decrees</unclear> <note>original Greek: "παρὰ τὰ Διατάγματα" (para ta diatagmata)</note>, beyond what has been established, even if he should prophesy, you should consider him a wolf who, under sheep's clothing, brings destruction and plague to the sheep. (Ignatius, Epistle 10 to Heron, Deacon of Antioch).

Therefore, no injustice is done to them if they are referred to and categorized among the number of the <term>heretics</term> <note>original Latin: "hereticos"</note>, for a <term>heretic</term> <note>original Latin: "hereticus"</note>—from the Greek word <unclear>choosing</unclear> <note>original Greek: "αἱρέσεως" (haireseōs)</note>, that is, "I choose," or in German *Ketzer* <note>The German word for heretic, "Ketzer," is historically derived from the "Cathars," a medieval sect.</note> as if from the Greek word for <unclear>pure</unclear> <note>original Greek: "καθαρός" (katharos). This refers to the Cathars' name for themselves, "the pure ones."</unclear>, or from the Hebrew <term>to pinch or cut off</term> <note>original Hebrew: "קָרַץ" (qāras)</note>, meaning he cut short, harvested, or cut off—is nothing other than an oddity or a newcomer who stubbornly and headstrongly defends and propagates his <term>paradoxes</term> and errors against the articles of faith, and separates and isolates himself from the true religion and other pure and unsuspected theologians. As Jerome also writes in his commentary on Galatians 5 (as found in Canon Law, Case 24, Question 3): "Whoever understands scripture differently than the sense of the Holy Spirit demands, by whom it was written, even if he has not withdrawn from the church, he can nonetheless be called a heretic." Likewise, Augustine teaches against the Manicheans (as cited in the same case and question): "Those who, within the Church of Christ, hold a diseased and perverse view, and if corrected so they might return to healthy wisdom, resist stubbornly and refuse to mend their pestilential and deadly dogmas but persist in defending them, they become heretics." One may read further on this in the Civil Law (Book 2, regarding heretics, Novel 109), and also in the writings of Theodoret (Dialogue 3), Augustine (*On True Religion*, Chapter 8), and Basil the Great.

# Book of Heroes

Chrysostom writes very elegantly about this in his 44th Homily on the *Incomplete Work*: <note>original Latin: "Si vestimentum emturus gyrat negotiatorem unum atq; alterum, & ubi meliores vestes invenerit, ab illo comparat, quomodo non oportet populum circumire omnes doctores, & inquirere ubi sincera veritas vendatur, & ubi corrupta & omnium confessiones audire, ac veriorem eligere, plus quàm vestimentum."</note> "If someone about to buy a garment visits one merchant and then another, and buys from the one where he has found the better clothes, how much more is it necessary for the people to go around to all the teachers and inquire where the sincere truth is sold, and where it is corrupted, and to hear the confessions of all and choose the one that is truer—even more so than for a garment."

->Question I.<-

## Why are they called New Prophets?

The word "Prophet" does not have just one sense, meaning, or understanding in Holy Scripture, but sometimes it aims and looks toward the prophesying of future things. In this sense, a prophet is nothing other than—and is so called—one who, through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, sees and proclaims beforehand what is to happen, just like the prophets of the Old Testament. In the New Testament, there was Agabus, who proclaimed the great famine <note>original Latin: "sub Claudio Imp. Act. 11." (under the Emperor Claudius, Acts 11)</note> and indicated the imprisonment and distress of Paul (*Acts 21*). Likewise, there was Anna (*Luke 2*) and the four daughters of Philip (*Acts 21*). For this reason, they were also called **videntes**, "Seers" or "Beholders," a word that is older than the word **Nabi**, or Prophet, as we read in *1 Samuel 9:9*: "He who today is called <term>נביא</term> (Nabi - prophet) was formerly called <term>ראה</term> (Roeh - seer)." Those whom we now call prophets were called seers in olden times. In Greek, the word is <term>προφήτης</term> (prophetes), from <term>πρόφημι</term> (prophemi), meaning "I foretell," or as others prefer, from <term>προφαίνω</term> (prophaino), which is "to show" <note>This etymology suggests that a prophet is one who reveals or makes visible the hidden things of God.</note>. From this, the temples were also called **Phana**. In Latin, they are called **vates**, almost like **fates** (diviners), from **fando** (speaking), though others may hold different views.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of prophecy. Having previously warned against "suspicious teachers," the author now defines the two ways the title of "Prophet" is used: first, as those who receive direct, supernatural revelations from God (the biblical prophets), and second, as those who interpret and explain Holy Scripture through the guidance of the Holy Spirit (theologians and teachers).</meta>

### From the Rose Garden

But the LORD God has revealed His will to these prophets either in a dream or in a vision, as it is written in Numbers 12:6: "If there is a prophet of the Lord among you, I will make myself known to him in a vision, or I will speak with him in a dream." The prophet Joel also says in chapter 2: "I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and daughters shall prophesy, your elders shall have dreams, and your young men shall see visions." And this is the provable distinction by which prophets are distinguished from other doctors and teachers: <note>original Latin: "Prophetæ enim, quia sunt servi DEI singulares non vulgares, solâ Dei instituuntur revelatione, Doctores autem scientiam sibi comparant summo studio & institutione."</note> "For prophets, because they are unique rather than ordinary servants of God, are instructed solely by the revelation of God; whereas Teachers acquire knowledge for themselves through the highest study and formal training."

Accordingly, every <term>Theologian</term> <note>Theologus: A scholar who specializes in the study of God and the interpretation of religious doctrines.</note> and teacher who explains the Scripture is called a prophet. This is explained and indicated not only by the ancient church father Ambrose <note>In Volume 3, page 239 of his works.</note> but also by the Apostle Paul in 1 Corinthians 14. And the word "prophet" <note>original Greek: "προφήτης"</note> signifies both a "foreteller of the future" and an "interpreter and steward of Scripture" <note>original Latin: "vaticinatorem, & Scripturæ interpretem ac procuratorem"</note>. Just as the prophets of the Old Testament prophesied through the prompting of the Holy Spirit (2 Peter 1), so too are pure and trustworthy teachers and theologians led by that same Spirit upon a level path (Psalm 143). For without the Holy Spirit, the Bible remains a sealed book to us (Isaiah 29, Revelation 5), and no one can call Jesus "Lord" except by the Spirit of God (1 Corinthians 12). Therefore, Augustine writes in Book 18, Chapter 38 <note>of "The City of God"</note>: <note>original Latin: "Existimo etiam ipsos quibus ea, quæ in autoritate religionis esse deberent, Sanctus utiq́ Spiritus revelabat, alia sicut homines historicâ diligentiâ, alia sicut Prophetas inspiratione divinâ scribere potuisse: atq́ hæc ita fuisse distincta, ut illa tamquam ipsis, ista verò tamquam Deo per ipsos loquenti judicarentur esse tribuenda, ac sic illa pertinerent ad ubertatem cognitionis, hæc ad religionis autoritatem, quâ autoritate custoditur Canon."</note> "I believe that those to whom the Holy Spirit revealed the things which belong to the authority of religion were able to write some things as men do with historical diligence, and other things as prophets do by divine inspiration. These were so distinct that the former were judged to be attributed to the men themselves, but the latter were attributed to God speaking through them. Thus, the former belong to the richness of knowledge, while the latter belong to the authority of religion—and it is by this authority that the Canon <note>The "Canon" refers to the official list of books recognized as genuine Holy Scripture.</note> is preserved."

### About the Rose Garden.

These newcomers <note>German: *newlinge*</note>, however—or these "New Prophets"—are not driven by the Holy Spirit, however much they may boast of it. **I.** Because Christ says that no man knows the time of the **Last Day**, nor can any man investigate or know it (Mark 13, Acts 1). The prophecy of these "New Prophets," however, serves *not for edification but rather for destruction* <note>original Latin: *ad ædificationem sed ad destructionem potius*</note>—not for improvement or comfort, but for a false sense of security and safety.

**III.** Those whom the Spirit of God drives do not lead anyone outside the boundaries and enclosure of God’s Word (Deuteronomy 13); *for everything we speak, we must affirm from Holy Scripture* <note>original Latin: *omne enim quom loquimur debemus affirmare de scriptura sancta*</note>, as Jerome says on Psalm 98. These New Prophets, however, lead people away from the clear letter of God’s Word toward their own conjectures, decrees, and dreams.

**IV.** All the Prophets and Apostles, and even Christ himself, prophesied about the state of sorrow that pious Christians would endure here on Earth—how they must have their <term>purgatory</term> <note>The author uses this term here not as the Catholic "place" of purging, but as a metaphorical "refining fire" of suffering on earth.</note> and **Fire of the Cross** <note>German: *Creutzfewr*; a term for the purifying trials of a believer.</note>, entering the Kingdom of God through much hardship and tribulation (Acts 14). **V.** Christ prophesies of war and rumors of war, which shall precede and happen before the Last Day, just as we have sufficiently experienced such things with particular heartache, crosses, and pain—

Furthermore, Paracelsus boasts that he was elected and chosen by GOD for this purpose: *to extinguish all the fantasies of devised and false works* <note>original Latin: "ut phantasias omnes excogitatorum & falsorum operum extingueret"</note>, in the preface to the book *On the Tincture of the Philosophers* <note>original Latin: "lib. de tinctura Physicor."</note> on page 249 of my edition. The Rosicrucians likewise boast and venture this, wanting not only to outsmart all the learned, but also to reform all estates—indeed, the whole world. And as Paracelsus writes in the said preface to *On the Tincture*, page 251: *I have a treasure in a certain city of Friuli, called Weiden in German, in the hospital, which neither the Roman lion nor the German Charles can pay for with their entire substance* <note>original Latin: "habeo thesaurum in quadam Friulorum civitate Weiden Germanicè dicta, in Xenodochio, quem nec leo Romanus nec Carolus Germanus tota sua substantia persolvere potest." The "Roman lion" refers to the Pope, and "German Charles" refers to Emperor Charles V.</note>. Thus also the Rosicrucians boast of their royal and princely palaces and treasures, and of the **Gold-making** <term>Gold-making: Alchemy or chrysopoeia, the supposed art of turning base metals into gold</term> (which they claim is a minor art); likewise, how they can heal all manner of diseases and maintain a person in fresh health for the duration of their life—yet they have never proven any of these things, nor have they actually performed or fulfilled them in practice.

Although many different judgments concerning the Order of the Rosicrucians have occurred to this day, we now see and understand from the published writings of Weigel <note>Valentin Weigel (1533–1588), a German theologian and mystic whose followers, "Weigelians," were often accused of heresy by the Lutheran establishment.</note>, Nagel <note>Paul Nagel (d. 1624), a German astronomer and mathematician known for his apocalyptic and mystical theories.</note>, Felgenhauer, and their like, that they are nothing but **Enthusiasts** <term>Enthusiasts: in this period, a derogatory term for those who believed they received direct divine inspiration apart from the Bible</term> and **Millenarians** <term>Millenarians (Chiliasten): those who believe in a future thousand-year reign of Christ on earth</term>; and the **Anabaptist** <term>Anabaptist: a radical religious group that rejected infant baptism, often viewed by the establishment as dangerous or subversive</term> spirit is also not far from them. But they call themselves Rosicrucians, not only because they wear a **Rose-Cross** <note>The Rose-Cross was the primary emblem of the Rosicrucian order, symbolizing the union of the rose (often signifying nature or the soul) and the cross (signifying the body or sacrifice).</note> for identification according to the nature and property of other orders—as appears in their *Fama* and *Confessio* <note>Referring to the *Fama Fraternitatis* (1614) and *Confessio Fraternitatis* (1615), the foundational manifestos of the Rosicrucian movement.</note>—but so that they might also hunt for glory with such a peculiar name, and thereby more quickly obtain assistance and approval from the people. Or else they delight in this name because they allegedly dream of an earthly Paradise and **Rose Garden**, and want to [restore] everything to the ancient, praiseworthy—

If it is not cured and healed right at the beginning, it eventually kills the person, as **Galen** <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–216 AD) was the most influential physician and medical researcher in the Roman Empire; his works remained the standard for medical knowledge through the Middle Ages and Renaissance.</note> indicates in his book *On Tumors Contrary to Nature*: **gangrene follows the greatest inflammations, which is indeed a certain mortification of the affected part; and unless it is cured very quickly, the affected part wastes away to such an extent that it invades other neighboring parts, and thus destroys the person.** <note>original Latin: "gangræna maximis succedit inflammationibus, quæ sanè mortificatio quædam adfectæ partis exsistit, & nisi curetur celerrimè usq; adeò pars adfecta extabescit, ut invadat alias continuas, atq; sic hominem perimat"</note>

Because the **disease of heresy** <note>The author uses "Ketzer Kranckheit" (heretic-sickness) to suggest that false belief is a contagious physiological and spiritual ailment.</note> eats away so much and clings so easily, we should not and must not be **dumb dogs** who refuse to bark (Isaiah 56). Although the Lord Christ most graciously promises and pledges that he will open to us when we knock, and hear us when we call (**Isaiah 65, Matthew 7**), this is not to be twisted or understood as if he should or would operate and work within us **directly** <note>original Greek: "ἀμέσως", meaning without any intermediate means or tools</note> without means. Keckermann <note>Bartholomäus Keckermann (1572–1609), a German Reformed theologian and philosopher known for his "analytical method."</note> writes in Book 1 of his *System of Theology*, chapter 4, page 57, that the light of the Holy Spirit is also ignited in the hearts of men through **logic** and **metaphysics**. Furthermore, Pelargus <note>Christoph Pelargus (1565–1633), a Lutheran theologian.</note>, in his *Commentary on John*, pages 7 and 8, proposes this **question** <note>original Latin: *quaestion.*</note>: whether the philosophers truly knew the **divine light** <note>original Greek: *φῶς divinum*</note>? And he answers **piously** <note>original Greek: *ὁσίως*</note> or tentatively: either that knowledge of **God** <note>original: *τοῦ θεοῦ*</note> was true and came either from a special revelation from God, or from the instruction of the Hebrews, the Egyptians, or the Sibyls <note>Ancient prophetesses believed by some early Christians to have foretold the coming of Christ to the pagans.</note>, or even from some suggestion of demons—or it was not true, which seems more likely from the example of Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish philosopher who sought to harmonize Greek philosophy with the Torah.</note> who followed the ways of Plato. Similarly, Amalric <note>Amalric of Bena (died c. 1206), a theologian whose followers, the Amalricians, were later condemned for pantheistic views.</note>—who was French by nationality, from the region of Chartres, and attained the laurel of the doctorate around the year of Christ 1204 in Paris—publicly taught that **God spoke just as much in Ovid as in Augustine** <note>original Latin: *quod Deus æquè fuerit locutus in Ovidio ac in Auguſtino*</note>, as reported by Caesarius in the 5th distinction of his *Book of Dialogues*.

In the same way, Antonio de Guevara also writes in the second part of his *Golden Epistles*, folio 5, that among the heathens some possessed the knowledge of the light, such as Socrates, who said in his **death-struggle** <note>original Latin: *in agone*</note> that he was ready to die in the knowledge of a single God; and Aristotle, who said in his death-struggle: "**Being of beings, have mercy on me**" <note>original Latin: *Ens entium miserere mei*</note>. And for this reason, Zwingli (in his *Confession to the King of France*, Volume 2, folio 559), Gualter (in his *Apology*), and the men of Emden (in the *Defense against Hunnius*, page 417) among the Calvinists—as well as Andrade (in his *Orthodox Explanations*, Book 3, page 288), Gregory of Valentia (Volume 3), Bellarmine (in *On Christ*, Book 1, chapter 3), and Gretser (in the *Book on the Holy Cross*, chapter 42) among the **papists** <note>original German: *pontificios*, a term used by Protestants to refer to Roman Catholics.</note>—have referred to and assigned the blind heathens to the number of the elect and blessed in eternal life. But **let us propose nothing without the Scriptures** <note>original Greek and Latin: *μηδὲν ἄτερ γραφῶν nihil sine scripturis*</note>.

# Concerning the Rose Garden

...briefly summarizes: to devote oneself to prayers, readings, and disputations <note>original Latin: *vacare orationibus, lectionibus & disputationibus*</note>. (From *On the Merits of the Church*, Chapter 31).

In former times, religious foundations <note>original: *Stiffte*; collegiate churches or endowed religious institutions</note> and monasteries were nothing other than gymnasiums, places of ascetic training, houses of contemplation <note>original Latin: *gymnasia, asceteria, phrontisteria*</note>, or schools of learning. (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, Chapters 5 and 11). These, however, have now become assembly-halls for monks and tabernacles for the beast <note>original Latin: *Monachorum conciliabula & Bestiae tabernacula*</note>, as Honorius of Autun <note>a 12th-century theologian</note> says in his *Dialogue on Predestination*: "where in the morning they sacrifice the son of the virgin at the altar, but at night they stir up the son of Venus <note>a reference to Roman goddess of love, implying sexual immorality</note> in the bedchamber; where by night they embrace Venus, and by day they venerate the virgin," according to Innocent [III] in his second sermon on Ash Wednesday. For they no longer wish to teach or learn in monasteries, but instead seek to earn heaven for themselves and others solely through their vows <note>original Latin: *votis*</note> and pledges. (References: Thomas Aquinas, 2. 2. question 88; Stapleton, *Antidote to the Gospel*, page 124; Clingius, *Summary of Doctrine*, page 523; Wimpina against Luther concerning monastic vows; John of Ghent in his *Compendium of Christian Doctrine*, section 34).

In former times, however, nothing was known or wanted to be known of such "vows and merits," because by these things God’s order, Christ’s merit, and the revealed Word of the LORD are profaned <note>original: *prophanirt*</note> and cast aside. Instead, the young clerics were simply masters of doctrine and witnesses of life <note>original Latin: *clerici Magistri doctrinae & testes vitae*</note>. This is where the offices of Dean and Scholaster <note>term: Scholaster; a high-ranking official responsible for the cathedral school</note> still get their names today. The church laws <note>original: *Canones*</note> also provide testimony and instruction on this matter (12. q. 1. c. *omnis aetas*, and *necessaria*. Also *de consecrat.* d. 1. c. *in omnibus*). They are also called monasteries <note>original: *Klöster*, related to the Latin *claustra* or enclosure</note> because they are meant to be "enclosures of virtues and teachings, not of vices and earned merits" <note>original Latin: *claustra virtutum & doctrinarum, non vitiorum & meritorum*</note>. Likewise, the word for Cathedral <note>original German: *Thum*, related to *Dom*</note> comes from "The Lord’s House" <note>original Latin: *Dominica*</note>, though others prefer to derive it from the Greek *tymbo* <note>original Greek: τυμβῷ, meaning a tomb or sacred mound</note>, signifying that they should be houses of God in which the Gospel shall be preached. (Eusebius, *Life of Constantine*, Book 4).

It is the same with human understanding; when a person is born, he is not immediately a *philosopher* <note>original: *Philosophus*</note>, nor does he have all kinds of arts and languages lying hidden within him. This is also the case with human understanding: when a person is born, he is not immediately a *philosopher*, nor does he have all kinds of arts and languages lying hidden within him; rather, he possesses only the *aptitude* <note>original: *aptitudo*; the natural capacity or potential</note> and capability to learn *philosophy* and other good arts. ...should say and affirm: Therefore, it follows undeniably that languages and arts are not in humans by nature; otherwise, they would sufficiently manifest themselves in *effect* <note>original Latin: *effectu*</note> and prove themselves.

II. That which must be learned and acquired through special sweat and diligence, great effort and care, and through much work and study, is certainly not in humans by nature, as all *philosophers* know—except for what *Cardanus* <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576) was a famous Italian physician and mathematician known for his eccentric theories.</note> says, namely that *man is impatient of labor* <note>original Latin: *hominem esse laboris impatientem*</note>, for which he is not unjustly laughed at and mocked by *Scaliger* <note>Julius Caesar Scaliger, a leading scholar of the time, who wrote a famous series of "Exercises" attacking Cardano's work.</note> in *Exercise 274*. Not a little work belongs to it when one wishes to become knowledgeable in languages and experienced in the arts; for here the *proverb* is *universally* <note>original Greek: *καθολικῶς* (katholikōs)</note> valid: *the gods sell good things for labor* <note>original Latin: *vendunt Di bona labore*</note>. And the more diligent one is, the sooner and the more one *profits* and increases: *With labor we learn, without labor we are ignorant; with labor we are vigorous, without labor we are sluggish.* <note>original Latin: *cum labore discimus, sine labore nescimus, cum labore strenui, sine labore inertes sumus*</note>

It follows thereafter irrefutably that because the arts and languages must be *acquired* <note>original: *acquirirt*</note> and attained through much work and study, they are certainly not in humans by nature. Whoever wishes to frame this concluding argument even more briefly can do so in this manner and *syllogize* <note>To form a <term>syllogism</term>, a logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two related premises.</note>: *Dispositions are not present by nature, but are acquired by frequent actions; arts are dispositions; therefore, they are not present by nature, but are acquired by frequent actions.* <note>original Latin: *Habitus non insunt naturâ, sed crebris actionibus comparantur, Artes sunt habitus, Ergò non insunt naturâ, sed crebris comparantur actionibus.*</note>

III. Those causes which work together at the same time *and produce one and the same effect* <note>original Latin: *& unum eundemque producunt effectum*</note> cannot be divided or separated from one another, *because joined causes acting in partnership are firm, while alone they achieve little or nothing* <note>original Latin: *quia conjunctae caußae in societate agentes firmae sunt, solae parum vel nihil efficiunt*</note>. Now, however, good arts and languages cannot be learned from nature alone without *discipline* and study, nor from *discipline* alone without nature; *therefore* <note>original: *Ergò*</note> these *allied causes* <note>original Latin: *caußae sociae*</note> should not be *separated* from one another, nor should the arts be attributed to nature alone.

## Question 5: Can one then not be taught through
## prayer and the anointing alone?

Regarding this, *Dr. Luther* <note>Martin Luther (1483–1546), the primary figure of the Protestant Reformation</note> gives us a magnificent and exceedingly beautiful report in the preface to the first German Volume of the Wittenberg and Jena editions: "I will show you," he says, "a right way to study *theology* <note>original: *Theologia*</note> in which I have practiced. There you will find three rules presented abundantly throughout the whole *Psalm*, and they are called: *Prayer, Meditation, and Trial* <note>original: *Oratio, Meditatio, Tentatio*. Therefore you see how David, in the aforementioned Psalm <note>Psalm 119</note>, so often complains about all sorts of enemies, insolent princes or tyrants, and about false spirits and sects <note>original: *Rotten*; referring to radical religious factions</note> that he must endure, because he *meditates*—that is, he occupies himself with God’s Word (as has been said) in all sorts of ways. If you follow this example well, you will also sing and boast with him in that same Psalm: *The law of your mouth is dearer to me than many thousands of pieces of gold and silver.* Likewise: *You make me wiser with your commandment than my enemies are, for it is my treasure forever.* *I am more learned than all my teachers, for your testimonies are my talk; I am wiser than the elders, for I keep your command.*

From this instruction and faithful counsel of the holy Luther, we see and understand that prayer is indeed highly necessary for study, so much so that without it, nothing fruitful can be started or completed in one's studies. For everything we do, in word and deed, should happen in the name of Jesus (Colossians 3). And if we lack wisdom, we should ask it of God (James 1). ### From the Rose Garden. ###

at the gathering in Schmalkalden <note>The Schmalkaldic League was a defensive alliance of Protestant princes in the 16th century.</note>, he wished "May God fill you with hatred for the Pope" <note>original: *impleat vos Deus odio papæ*</note>; so too do I wish for all of you, "that God may fill you with hatred for the Enthusiasts and all heretics" <note>original: *ut Deus vos impleat odio Enthusiastarum omniumq́ue hæreticorum*</note>.

But Paulus Felgenhauer <note>A controversial Bohemian visionary and writer (1593–1677) who advocated for direct spiritual revelation.</note>, in his *Mirror of the Times* at section E. ij., brings forward as proof and example the prophet Daniel; he says that Daniel studied for three years in the school of the Holy Spirit, and after those three years he was more skilled than all the scholars in the King's realm. Therefore, he claims, if one were to study today in this school of Daniel or the Holy Spirit, one could learn more in two or three years than a thousand students combined, even if they remained at the universities for a hundred years and studied day and night. Likewise, the example of the Apostles might also be introduced and cited, upon whom the Holy Spirit was poured out on the great day of Pentecost, giving them the power to speak of the **mighty works of God** <note>original: *magnalia Dei*</note> (Acts 2).

To this we answer: it is a **fallacy of division** <note>original: *sophisma divisionis*; a logical error where one separates things that belong together—in this case, separating the Holy Spirit's guidance from the actual physical study Daniel performed.</note>, for Daniel was not only in the school of the Holy Spirit, but he also studied in the schools of the Chaldeans, and learned Chaldean writing and language from his **teachers** <note>original: *præceptoren*</note> (Daniel 1:4). And through such means, God the Lord gave him skill and understanding in all kinds of writing and wisdom, and in all visions and dreams (Daniel 1:17). Likewise, the Apostles were in Christ’s school and were orally instructed by him for three and a half years. From this, it appears that the cited examples do not support, but rather hinder and oppose their "Enthusiasm" <note>The belief that God speaks directly to the heart without needing the Bible or the Church.</note>.

11. Furthermore, these are **unique examples, which are not to be drawn into imitation** <note>original: *Exempla singularia, quæ non trahuntur in imitationem*; a legal and theological principle that a miracle or special case does not set a general rule for everyone else.</note>. For although the Lord called the Prophets and Apostles without external means, and poured out the Holy Spirit upon them in a miraculous and visible way, He does not wish to deal with us in such a manner—without means—in these latter days. Instead, He works through the Word, and no longer through light and visions, or through the **Urim and Thummim** <note>Sacred devices used by ancient Hebrew priests to determine God's will.</note> as in the Old Testament (Exodus 28).

## Q. 6 Does one then need no books for studying?

Weigelius <note>Valentin Weigel (1533–1588), a German mystic and theologian whose "Enthusiast" views suggested that internal spiritual revelation was superior to external study.</note> says that for **true Theology** one does not need a great multitude of books; rather, one book is enough—namely the **Bible**—for anyone who can read it or hear it read; as seen in his *Treatise on Universal Study, chapter 7.* <note>original: "in tr. de studio univers. cap. 7."</note> Likewise, Paulus Felgenhauer <note>A radical Bohemian reformer and contemporary of the author known for his visionary writings.</note> writes the same in his *Mirror of the Times,* part B. ij. <note>original: "Zeitspiegel lit. B. ij."</note>

However, we rightly make a distinction between a <term>theologian by profession</term> and a <term>theologian by confession</term>. <note>The author distinguishes between those who study theology as a career (profession) and lay Christians who simply profess their faith (confession).</note> For although the "confessional" theologians—which includes all Christians, as St. Peter says in *1 Peter 2:9*—do not require many books, but instead find satisfaction in the Bible and a few other books (or, if they cannot read, they hear God’s word and preserve it in a fine, good heart so that it brings forth fruit with patience, *Luke 8*); nevertheless, necessity demands that the **professional theologians**—those who must read, preach, and write for others—be supplied with more books, according to each one’s opportunity. For **books are the nearest instruments, divinely given, for propagating and preserving wisdom and prudence among the human race**, as Keckermann <note>Bartholomäus Keckermann (1572–1609), a German Reformed theologian and philosopher known for his "System" of various sciences.</note> says in his *System of Politics, Book 1, page 325.* <note>original: "libri enim sunt proxima instrumenta & divinitus data ad sapientiam prudentiamq. in genere humano propagandam & conservandam, ut ait Keckerm. lib. 1. Syst. Polit. pag. 325."</note>

For this reason, Sirach says in Chapter 39: "Whoever devotes himself to learning the law of the Most High must seek out the wisdom of all the ancients and study the prophets. He must observe the history of famous people and reflect upon them—what they mean and what they teach; he must learn spiritual proverbs and practice the deepest sayings." For how shall one teach others who has learned and read nothing himself beforehand? How shall one instruct others who knows nothing himself? And how shall he know and learn if he does not have his **living and silent teachers**? <note>original: "vivos & mutos preceptores." A common humanist phrasing where "living teachers" are professors and "silent teachers" are books.</note> Thus, the **Fathers** and **Church Fathers** did not only exercise and practice themselves in the Bible, but also read and re-read the writings of other people, so that they might "test everything and hold fast only to that which is good." <note>A reference to the biblical mandate in 1 Thessalonians 5:21.</note>

**Holy Scripture**, however, points us nowhere else but to **Christ** alone; Him we shall hear, according to *Matthew 3 and 17*. And even the Canon Law <note>original: "Geistliche Recht"</note> points us to **Christ** Himself, and not to the *writings of the fathers* <note>original Latin: "scripta patrum"</note>. For *if Christ alone is to be heard*, as it is said in Distinction 8, Chapter 9: *we ought not to attend to what someone before us thought should be done, but what Christ, who is before all, did first.* <note>original Latin: "si enim solus Christus audiendus est... non debemus attendere, quid aliquis ante nos faciendum putaverit, sed quid, qui ante omnes est, Christus prior fecerit."</note> So also writes **Augustine** in his 19th Epistle: *I have learned to yield this honor and reverence only to the books of Scripture which are now called Canonical; I firmly believe that none of their authors made any error in writing. Others I read in such a way that, no matter how much they excel in holiness and doctrine, I do not therefore think a thing true because they thought so, but because they were able to persuade me—either through those Canonical authors or by probable reason—that it does not depart from the truth.* <note>original Latin: "Solis scripturarum libris... didici hunc honorem actimorem deferre... alios ità lego... non ideo verum putem, quia ipsi ita senserunt..."</note>

Accordingly, regarding the vast multitude of books, we maintain this distinction: we do not advise the studying youth to overwhelm themselves with various **authors** right at the beginning. Rather, the <term>students of theology</term> <note>original: "studiosi Theologiæ"</note> must, above all things, drive and rub the **Bible**—reading and re-reading it—so that they might become good <term>textualists</term> <note>original: "textuales"; meaning scholars who are intimately familiar with the primary biblical text itself.</note>.

### 27. Do effort and labor also belong to studying?

Although it is not praiseworthy, it is nonetheless a lovely, sweet, and pleasant thing that these **New Heavenly Prophets** <note>A derogatory term for radical reformers and mystics who claimed to receive direct revelation from God without the need for traditional study.</note> present to the studying youth. Therefore, it is no wonder or cause for surprise if many of them ally themselves with them and become bound to their **enthusiasm** <note>original: "Enthusiasterey"; in the 17th century, this referred to a belief in private, direct divine inspiration over the authority of Scripture.</note>. For **Weigel** <note>Valentin Weigel (1533–1588), a German mystic whose writings suggested that true knowledge comes from an "inner light" rather than external books.</note> says in his *Treatise on Universal Study*, letter H: That one can learn everything *without study and labor* <note>original Latin: "sine studio & labore"</note> if one only prays. Praying is studying **theology**, and studying **theology** is praying. As much effort and labor as belongs to **theology**, so much belongs to prayer—which is to say, none at all: *nothing is easier than to pray, to use sweet leisure, and to enjoy sweet silence.* <note>original Latin: "nihil facilius quam orare, quàm suavi otio uti, frui silentio dulci."</note>

Furthermore, prayer is not as easy or insignificant as **Weigel** considers it to be; rather, it is at once difficult and bitter, since the **Devil**, along with his tender bride and wicked skin—the decadent, contemptible, and desolate world—always winds himself into it to hinder and hamper the *Cantate* <note>Latin for "Sing" or "Song"; likely referring to the prayerful worship or spiritual "song" of the believer.</note> of pious Christians through many types of tricks and ruses. Moreover, the **Adamic man** <note>A theological term for human beings in their natural, fallen state, inherited from Adam, which is seen as inherently incapable of true spiritual work without grace.</note> is not in the least qualified or fit for this, because prayer, if it is to be heard, must happen in the name of **Christ** (*John 16*). Of this, flesh and blood know nothing (*Matthew 16*). Thus, a fire-zealous, unfeigned **faith** must also be added...

### Question 9: Does the student <note>original Latin: *discens*</note>, or one who learns, become essentially one with that which he learns?

Although the clear distinction between **substance** and **accident** <term>In traditional logic and philosophy, "substance" is the essential nature of a person or thing, while an "accident" is a quality (like knowledge or skill) that can be added or removed without changing what the thing is.</term> is known and recognized by everyone, nevertheless these "New Heavenly Prophets" are not in the least bit shy or ashamed to propagate such a **confused chaos** <note>original Latin: *confusum chaos*</note> within precious Christendom, and to mix the student <note>original Latin: *discentem*</note> with the subject being learned <note>original Latin: *discendo*</note>. "To teach and to study is precisely to become that which we learn, and to recognize that which we are: just as he who learns to know the Son of God becomes that which he learns, namely a Christian, a child of God; and he who learns **dialectic** <note>the art of logical reasoning and debate</note> becomes a **dialectician**. However, it is unnecessary to **refute** this new and previously unheard-of **paradox** <note>original Latin: *Paradoxon prolixè zu refutiren*</note> at great length, especially since Weigel provides neither grounds nor reasons for it. Furthermore, it is impossible to prove either from God’s Word or with philosophical foundations. For Holy Scripture teaches us that in the Creator alone, and not in the creature—in God and not in man—everything is essential and nothing is accidental <note>meaning God is His own attributes, whereas human traits are separate from their essence</note>. As the Lord himself said to Moses in Exodus 3: **"This is my name: I shall be who I shall be."**

# Book of Heroes

...he becomes a **logician** <note>original: *Dialecticus*</note>, and whoever learns **Christ** and remains steadfast in faith in Him is a **Christian** and a child of God. Such words were correctly positioned and introduced **in the concrete** <note>original: *in concrete*</note> by Weigel; and if one agrees with such an opinion, then this is the best advice: **"that he correct his tongue and hold his mind; for a concept is not attributed univocally to God and to creatures, as those fools Duns Scotus, Antonius Andreas, William of Ockham, and Gabriel Biel suggest."** <note>original Latin: *ut corrigat linguam & teneat mentem: non enim univocus conceptus Deo & creaturis attribuitur, ut ineptiunt Scot...* The author is attacking the Scholastic idea that words like "being" mean the same thing when applied to God and to humans.</note>

Rather, there remains the **difference** and distinction: that God and everything within Him is essence itself, but in humans, there is not only the **substance of soul and body**, but there are also the **accidents** <note>In philosophy, "accidents" are qualities (like knowledge or color) that can change without changing the fundamental nature of the thing.</note> within him, which are not essentially one, nor are they essentially united with the human being, as can be **demonstrated** and clearly illustrated **as plain as day.** <note>original Greek: ὀφθαλμοφανερῶς (*ophthalmophaneros*), meaning "visibly" or "before one's eyes."</note>

1. Whoever is essentially one and united with **Christ** when he learns **Christ** is not only a child of God, but he is also **Christ** himself; for that is what essential **union** and unity is capable of: **"unity is an affection of being, or the same thing as entity"** <note>original Latin: *unitas est affecta entis, aut eadem res cum entitate*</note> (Scaliger, *Exercise 105, section 2*). Thus, if someone reads in a book and becomes essentially one and united with the book, an essential transformation occurs, so that either the reader is essentially transformed into the book or the book into the reader, and the two become essentially one with each other. This is just as Cedrenus, Epiphanius (in the *Life of Daniel*), and Rupert of Deutz (Book 6 of *On the Victory of the Word*, Chapter 29) write of King Nebuchadnezzar, that he was transformed into an ox and a lion. Or how **Circe** **mutated** Odysseus's companions into pigs in **Homer** (see Augustine, *The City of God*, Book 18, Chapters 10 and 18). Or also as the Papists <note>original: *Päbstler*, a derogatory term used by Reformers for Roman Catholics.</note> feign regarding the **transubstantiation** <note>original Greek: <unclear>μευσίαν</unclear>, likely *metousian* or *metousis* (change of essence).</note> **in the Supper**, that bread and wine are **transubstantiated** and essentially transformed into **Christ’s** body and blood (*The Fortress of Faith*, Book 3, Consideration 4, folio 105; Michael Lochmayer, Volume 9, *Parochial Cures*, Chapter 3; Schæpper, *Institutions*, page...)
