<meta>This page continues the logical and theological refutation of Valentin Weigel's mysticism. On the previous page, the author argued that while a person becomes a "Christian" by learning about Christ, they do not literally become the "substance" of Christ. Here, the author uses Aristotelian logic to prove that knowledge is an "accident" (a quality) rather than a "substance" (the thing itself).</meta>

# From the Rose Garden <note>original: *Vom Rosengarten.* This title likely refers to a specific collection of theological arguments or a section of the larger work.</note>

130. *Martin Becanus, Volume 2, pages 268 and 299. Gregory de Valentia, on transubstantiation, chapter 2.* <note>These are citations to contemporary Catholic theologians whom the author is likely using as authorities on the definition of "substance."</note> Now, however, it can never be proven in all eternity that a person, through their reading and studying, should be transformed into Christ and become essentially one with Him; otherwise, there would certainly not be one Christ, but many thousands of different Christs; or else the one Christ would have been essentially transformed into so many thousands of people who have recognized and learned of Him, which is quite abominable and blasphemous to hear. Likewise, it is unheard of and unprovable that the learner and reader should essentially become the book that he has read and learned, or that the book should be essentially transformed into the person and become one with him according to its essence. Therefore, it is a completely absurd and unscriptural blasphemy when **Weigel** <note>Valentin Weigel (1533–1588) was a German theologian and mystic whose ideas about "internal word" and mystical union with God were highly controversial among orthodox Lutherans.</note> writes thoughtlessly, not only in the words cited, but also *in his treatise on universal study, chapter 3*: "Whoever studies Christ is essentially united with Him; for studying is truly nothing else than the essential union of the learner with the learned."

II. What is accidental cannot belong to the essence of a thing, **"for a substance can never be made from an accident, nor an accident from a substance; likewise, an accident does not constitute the essence of a thing."** <note>original Latin: *ex accidente enim nunquam potest fieri substantia...* Here the author uses Aristotelian logic: a "substance" is what a thing is, while an "accident" is a quality it has. For example, a man is a substance, but his "knowledge of music" is an accident—if he forgets the music, he is still a man.</note> *Aristotle, Metaphysics Book 7, Section 37. Scaliger, Exercise 10. Zabarella, Book on the Constitution of the Individual, Chapter 4.* <note>The author cites the giants of classical and Renaissance logic to prove his point.</note> Now, however, that which one reads, studies, and learns from books is an accidental thing; **"all arts and sciences are accidents: Therefore they cannot enter the essence of man, or be essentially exchanged and united with man."** <note>original Latin: *omnes artes & scientiae sunt accidentia...*</note>

III. **"Every accident exists in a substance inherently as in its subject; every art is an accident; Therefore it exists inherently in the substance, and consequently, if it exists in the substance, it is not (nor does it become) the substance itself through essential union or mutation."** <note>This is a formal syllogism in Latin. The author is saying that knowledge (the accident) lives "inside" the person (the substance), but they remain two different categories of being. Knowing about Christ does not turn your human DNA into "Christ-substance."</note>

<header>Book of Heroes</header>

...one becomes a **logician** <note>original: *Dialecticus*</note>, and whoever learns Christ and steadfastly believes in Him is a Christian and a child of God. Such words are correctly used and introduced by **Weigel** in concrete terms; and if he agrees with this opinion, then the best advice is: *that he should correct his speech and hold his mind in check: for a univocal concept is not attributed to both God and creatures, as Scotus and others foolishly claim.* <note>Latin: *ut corrigat linguam & teneat mentem: non enim univocus conceptus Deo & creaturis attribuitur, ut ineptiunt Scot...* The author is citing a technical debate in Scholastic philosophy: "univocity" is the idea that words like "existence" mean the same thing when applied to God as to humans, which the author here rejects.</note>

Rather, the difference and distinction remains: that God, and everything that is in Him, is the **Essence** <note>original: *Wesen*</note> itself. But in humans, there is not only the **substance** <note>The underlying reality of a thing.</note> of the soul and body, but there are also **accidents** <note>term: *accidentis* — In Aristotelian logic, these are qualities or properties (like knowledge or color) that can change without changing the essential nature of the person.</note> within him, which are not essentially one with the person, nor are they essentially united with him, as can be <greek>evidently demonstrated</greek> <note>original Greek: *ὀφθαλμοφανῶς* (ophthalmophanōs), meaning "visible to the eye."</note> and clearly explained.

1. Whoever becomes essentially one and united with Christ when he learns Christ, is not only a child of God, but he is also Christ himself. For that is what an essential union and unity allows: *unity is a property of being, or the same thing as entity.* <note>Latin: *unitas est affecta entis, aut eadem res cum entitate* (attributed to Scaliger).</note> Thus, if someone reads in a book and becomes essentially one and united with the book, an essential **transformation** occurs, so that either the reader is essentially transformed into the book, or the book into the reader, and the two become essentially one with each other. This is just as **Cedrenus**, **Epiphanius** (in *The Life of Daniel*), and **Rupert of Deutz** <note>original: *Rupertus Tuicens.*</note> write of King **Nebuchadnezzar**, saying that he was transformed into an ox and a lion; or how **Circe** changed the companions of **Ulysses** into swine in the works of **Homer**; or even how the Papists invent the <greek>change of essence</greek> <note>original Greek: *μετουσίας* (metousias), referring to the Catholic doctrine of the Eucharist.</note> at the Last Supper, claiming that the bread and wine are **transubstantiated** and essentially transformed into Christ’s body and blood.

This page uses Aristotelian logic to argue that knowledge is a quality one possesses, not a change to one's fundamental being.</meta>

### Of the Rose Garden.

<margin>130. Becanus, Volume 2, pages 268 & 297. Gregory of Valencia, *On Transubstantiation*, chapter 2.</margin> Now, however, it can never be proven in all eternity that a person, through their reading and studying, should be transformed into Christ and become **essentially** one with Him. If that were the case, there would certainly not be just one Christ, but many thousands of different Christs; or else the one and only Christ would have been essentially transformed into so many thousands of people who have known and learned of Him, which is quite abominable and blasphemous to hear. So too is it unheard of and unprovable that the learner and reader should essentially become the book that he has read and learned, or that the book should be essentially transformed into the person and become one with him according to its essence. Therefore, it is a completely absurd and unscriptural blasphemy when **Weigel**—not only in the words previously cited, but also *in his treatise on universal study, Chapter 3*—thoughtlessly writes: "Whoever studies Christ becomes essentially united with Him, for studying is truly nothing other than the essential union of the learner with that which is learned."

**II.** Whatever is **accidental** <note>original: *zufellig*. In this context, it refers to "accidents" in logic—qualities like "being tall" or "knowing math" that can change without the person ceasing to be a human.</note> cannot belong to the **essence** <note>The fundamental nature of what a thing is.</note> of a thing; *for a substance can never be made from an accident, nor an accident from a substance; likewise, an accident does not constitute the essence of a thing.* <note>Latin: *ex accidente enim numquam potest fieri substantia, neq; ex substantia accidens; Item accidens non constituit rei essentiam...* The author is quoting Aristotelian principles used in university debates of the time.</note> **Aristotle**, *Metaphysics* Book 7, Contrast 37; **Scaliger**, Exercise 10; **Zabarella**, *On the Constitution of Individuals*, chapter 4. Now, however, that which one reads, studies, and learns from books is an accidental thing; *all arts and sciences are accidents: therefore they cannot enter into the essence of a human, or be essentially exchanged and united with a human.* <note>Latin: *omnes artes & scientiæ sunt accidentia: Ergo non possunt hominis essentiam ingredi, aut cum homine essentialiter commutari & uniri.*</note>

**III.** *Every accident exists in a substance inherently, as if in a subject; every art is an accident; therefore it exists inherently in the substance, and consequently, if it exists in the substance, it is not—nor does it become—the substance itself through essential union or mutation.* <note>Latin: *Omne accidens est in substantia inhæshivè tamquam in subjecto, omnis ars est accidens, Ergo inhæshivè inest in substantia...* This is a syllogism, a formal logical argument: if knowledge is a property (accident) and the human is the reality (substance), the property is "inside" the person but does not "become" the person.</note>

# Book of Heroes <note>The header "Heldenbuch" (Book of Heroes) appears in this edition, though the text is a continuation of Martin Luther’s 1524 treatise addressed to German councilmen regarding the establishment of Christian schools.</note>

Therefore the Apostles themselves deemed it necessary to set down the New Testament in the **Greek language** and bind it there, doubtless to keep it safe and certain for us, as if in a holy ark. For they saw everything that was to come, and which has now come to pass: that if it were kept only in men’s heads, many wild and desolate disorders and mixtures—so many different opinions, obscurities, and teachings—would arise in Christendom. There would be no way to resist these, nor to protect the simple-hearted, if the **New Testament** were not securely contained in writing and language. Therefore, it is certain that where languages do not remain, the Gospel must ultimately perish.

This has also been proven, and experience still shows it; for soon after the time of the Apostles, when the languages ceased, the Gospel, the faith, and all of **Christendom** also began to [ever more...] <note>The text ends mid-sentence with "je=" (ever). In the original treatise, the sentence concludes that Christendom "declined more and more."</note>

<summary>Luther argues that languages like Greek and Hebrew are the essential containers for the Gospel, warning that their neglect leads to spiritual and intellectual "beastliness." He asserts that the Apostles wrote the New Testament in Greek specifically to prevent the doctrinal chaos that occurs when scripture is passed down only by memory or oral tradition.</summary>

# Of the Rose Garden <note>The header "Vom Rosengarten" (Of the Rose Garden) likely refers to the title of a specific section or perhaps the specific edition’s grouping; however, the content remains part of Luther’s 1524 treatise on schools.</note>

...more and more, until it sank under the Pope, and since the languages declined during that time, nothing particularly special was seen in Christendom; instead, many horrible abominations occurred because of ignorance of the languages. Now, conversely, since the languages have come forth, they bring such a light with them and do such great things that the whole world wonders and must confess that we have the Gospel as clear and pure, almost as the Apostles had it. It has come fully into its original purity, and is much purer than it was in the time of St. Jerome or Augustine. In short, the Holy Spirit is no fool; He does not deal in trivial or unnecessary things. He considered languages so useful and necessary for Christendom that He often brought them with Him from heaven <note>A reference to the Pentecost, where the Apostles were granted the "gift of tongues" (Acts 2).</note>, which alone should move us enough to seek them with diligence and honor, and not to despise them, since He has now awakened them again on earth.

"Yes," you say, "many Church Fathers attained salvation and also taught without the languages." That is true. But how do you account for the fact that they often erred in the Scriptures? How often does St. Augustine fail in the Psalms and other interpretations, as well as Hilary—indeed, all who have ventured to interpret the Scriptures without the languages? And even if they happened to speak correctly, they were still not certain of the matter—whether the meaning truly belonged to the passage where they applied it. Let me show an example of this: It is rightly said that Christ is the Son of God. But how mocking it sounds to the ears of the adversaries <note>In this context, "adversaries" often refers to Jewish scholars or critics of the Reformation who were fluent in Hebrew.</note> when people base this on the 110th Psalm: "With thee is the beginning in the day of thy power" <note>original Latin: *Tecum principium in die virtutis tuae*. In the Latin Vulgate used by the medieval Church, this was interpreted as a reference to the divine origin of Christ. Luther argues that the Hebrew text does not support this specific theological reading.</note>, even though in the Hebrew language nothing about the Godhead is written there. When one protects the faith with such uncertain grounds and misspoken arguments, is it not a shame and a mockery of Christ in the eyes of the adversaries who are knowledgeable in the language?

# Heldenbuch <note>The header "Heldenbuch" (Book of Heroes) indicates this page may come from an anthology or a specific collection, though the text continues Martin Luther's 1524 treatise on education.</note>

...and they only become more stubborn in their error, and look upon our faith as a human dream, despite its good appearance.

Whose fault is it now that our faith is brought to such shame? It is because we do not know the languages; and there is no help here except to know the languages. Was St. Jerome <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420 AD) was the scholar who translated the Bible into Latin, known as the Vulgate.</note> not forced to translate the Psalter anew from the Hebrew for this very reason? Because whenever we deal with the Jews using our version of the Psalter, they mock us, saying that the Hebrew does not say what our people claim it does. Now, the interpretations of all the ancient Church Fathers who handled the Scripture without the languages (though they may teach nothing wrong) are of such a nature that they very often use uncertain, uneven, and inappropriate language. Even St. Augustine himself must confess, as he writes in *On Christian Doctrine* <note>original: "de doctr. Christiana". Augustine's foundational work on how to study and teach the Bible.</note>, that a Christian teacher who is to interpret the Scripture needs the Greek and Hebrew languages in addition to Latin. Otherwise, it is impossible for him not to stumble everywhere—indeed, there is still difficulty and labor even if one knows the languages well.

Therefore, there is a great difference between a simple <note>original: "schlechten," which in Luther’s time meant "simple" or "plain," rather than "bad."</note> preacher of the faith and an interpreter of the Scripture, or as St. Paul calls it, a "prophet." A simple preacher (it is true) has enough clear sayings and texts through translations that he can understand Christ, teach and live holily, and preach to others. But to interpret the Scripture and to handle it on his own, and to struggle against those in error—as a leader of the Scripture, he is too inadequate. That cannot be done without the languages. Now, one must certainly have such "prophets" in Christendom who study and interpret the Scripture, and who are also fit for battle; it is not enough merely to live holily and teach rightly. Therefore, the languages are absolutely and in all things necessary in Christendom,

### Of the Rose Garden <note>The header "Vom Rosengarten" (Of the Rose Garden) likely refers to the title of a specific section in this anthology, though the text continues Martin Luther’s 1524 treatise *To the Councilmen of all Cities in Germany that they Establish and Maintain Christian Schools*.</note>

...just as the prophets or interpreters; although it is not necessary, nor must it be, that every Christian or preacher should be such a prophet as St. Paul says in 1 Corinthians 12 and Ephesians 4.

This is the reason why, since the time of the Apostles, the Scripture has remained so obscure, and no certain, steady interpretations have been written about it. For even the holy Fathers (as has been said) often failed; and because they were ignorant of the languages, they are rarely of one mind—one teaches this way, another that way. St. Bernard <note>St. Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153) was a highly influential mystic and monk, whom Luther often praised for his piety while criticizing his allegorical style of interpretation.</note> was a man of such great spirit that I would almost venture to set him above all famous teachers, both old and new. But look how often he plays with the Scripture (albeit in a spiritual way) and leads it away from its true meaning. Therefore, the Sophists <note>Luther used "Sophists" as a derogatory term for the Scholastic theologians of the Middle Ages, whom he accused of using complex, circular logic to obscure simple biblical truths.</note> have also said that the Scripture is obscure; they believed that God’s Word was by nature so dark and spoke so strangely. But they do not see that the entire fault lies with the languages. Otherwise, nothing simpler has ever been spoken than God’s Word—if only we understood the languages. A Turk must surely speak "darkly" to me, yet a Turkish child of seven years understands him well, simply because I do not know the language.

Therefore, it was also a foolish undertaking to try to learn the Scripture through the interpretations of the Fathers and by reading many books and glosses <term>glosses: brief marginal or interlinear explanations of words in a text, which became the standard way of studying the Bible in the Middle Ages</term>. One should instead have devoted oneself to the languages. For the dear Fathers, because they were without the languages, sometimes labored over a single passage with many words, and yet they barely scraped by—half-guessing and half-failing. Thus you run after them with much effort, when you could have interpreted it much better yourself through the languages than the one you are following. For as the sun is compared to a shadow, so is the [original] language compared to all the glosses of the Fathers.

Since it then now behooves Christians [to know] the Holy Scripture—

## Schoolbook

...to study as their very own unique book. It is a sin and a shame that we do not know our own book, nor understand our God’s language and Word. It is an even greater sin and shame that we do not learn languages, especially now that God offers them to us and provides teachers, books, and everything necessary—almost enticing us to do so, for He wants His book to be open to all. Oh, how joyful the dear Fathers would have been if they could have approached the Holy Scripture and learned the languages as easily as we can! With great toil and diligence, they barely managed to obtain the crumbs, whereas we, with half—indeed, with almost no labor—could win the whole loaf of bread. Oh, how their diligence shames our laziness! Indeed, how sternly God will judge such lack of effort and ingratitude on our part.

This is also why St. Paul, in 1 Corinthians 14, desires that within Christendom there should be a judgment <note>Luther emphasizes that the congregation or other scholars must be able to "judge" or evaluate whether a preacher's interpretation is accurate to the original text.</note> concerning all kinds of teaching. For this purpose, it is absolutely necessary to know the languages. For a preacher or teacher may well read the Bible <note>original: "Biblia"</note> through and through as much as he wants; he may hit or miss the mark if no one is there to judge whether he does it correctly or not. If one is to judge, then there must be skill or knowledge of languages present; otherwise, all is lost. 

Therefore, although faith and the Gospel <note>original: "Evangelium"</note> may be preached by plain preachers without languages, such preaching is nevertheless sluggish and weak, and eventually, people grow tired and weary of it, and it falls to the ground. But where the languages are present, there the work proceeds fresh and strong; the Scripture is thoroughly searched, and faith is ever renewed through more and more words and works. For this reason, Psalm 129 <note>Luther is using the Vulgate numbering; this imagery of "opening the thicket" is often associated with his interpretation of Psalm 29:9, where the voice of the Lord "makes the deer calve and discovers the thick bushes."</note> compares such study of the Scripture to a hunt, saying that God opens the thick pasture to the hinds. And Psalm 1 compares it to a tree that is always green and always has fresh water.

While Luther admired their survival under persecution, he criticized their lack of linguistic scholarship, which he felt left them vulnerable to error.</note>, who do not [regard] the languages...

...to be considered proper. But dear friend, "Spirit" this or "Spirit" that—I have also been in the Spirit and have indeed seen the Spirit (if one is to boast of one’s own flesh). Perhaps I have seen more of it in a year than those boasters will see in their whole lives, however much they brag. This much I know for certain: however much the Spirit does everything alone, I would have been far out of range <note>original: "allen Puischen zu ferne," an idiom meaning he would have been ineffective or unable to reach his target</note> if the languages had not helped me and made me sure and certain of the Scripture. The Devil does not fear my spirit nearly as much as he fears my language and pen when applied to the Scripture. For my spirit takes nothing from him except myself alone; however, the <term>Holy Scripture</term> and the languages make the world too narrow for him and cause great damage to his kingdom.

In this regard, I cannot praise the <term>Waldensian</term> <note>original: "Brüder Valdenses." A medieval Christian movement that lived in poverty and translated the Bible into vernacular languages, but lacked the scholarly training in Greek and Hebrew that Luther championed.</note> brothers at all for despising the languages. For even if they teach correctly, they must very often miss the true meaning of the text and remain unequipped and unskilled to fight for the faith against error. Furthermore, their way of speaking is so obscure and phrased in such a peculiar manner—distanced from the scriptural way of speaking—that I fear it is not, or will not remain, pure. It is very dangerous to speak about God's matters in a different way or with different words than those which God Himself uses. In short: they may live and teach holily for themselves; but because they remain without the languages, they will necessarily lack what all others lack—namely, they cannot handle the Scripture with certainty and depth, nor can they be useful to other nations. Since they are perfectly capable of doing this but choose not to, they must consider how they will answer for it before God.

## Q 11. Is it also necessary that one learns Grammar, Dialectic, and Rhetoric from youth?

Since these <term>Enthusiastic</term> <note>From the German "Enthusiastische," referring to radical reformers who believed they received direct, "inspired" revelations from God apart from the written Bible</note> newcomers want to reform the entire world and outsmart all the learned scholars, it is highly surprising that they reject the languages and arts through which God the Lord has given, spread, and preserved the Gospel. Without these, the Scripture cannot be explained in its proper sense and understanding, nor can opposing doctrines and errors be refuted. Indeed, without the knowledge of languages and without the cognition and science of the arts, there is nothing in the world but pure darkness and **mere ignorance; for languages are the gateways to all disciplines, and he who repudiates languages detracts from all arts and disciplines.** <note>original Latin: "et mera ignorantia quippe linguæ sunt fores omnium disciplinarum, & qui linguas repudiat, omnes artes ac disciplinas detractat"</note> Wherefore we also conclude and judge—because <term>Weigel</term> <note>Valentin Weigel (1533–1588), a German theologian and mystic whose writings suggested that true knowledge comes from an "inner light" rather than external study</note> in his *Treatise on Universal Study*, chapter 7, rejects the languages and fine arts—that those who reject Grammar, Rhetoric, and Dialectic either live in darkness (as is plain as day) or that they wish to admit nothing but **brothers of ignorance** <note>original Latin: "fratres ignorantiæ"</note> into their order, so that their "Enthusiastic" horrors and abominations might not become known and recognized.

For regarding these three philosophical instruments or arts—Grammar, Logic, and Rhetoric—one can correctly say that they are **the foundations of all disciplines.** <note>original Latin: "omnium disciplinarum fundamenta"</note> Whoever rejects or despises them also despises or rejects everything that may be built upon such a foundation, **and moves about in other sciences like a stranger in an unknown region.** <note>original Latin: "& versatur in cæteris scientijs, ut hospes in regione ignotâ"</note> As <term>Jerome</term> <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the Church Father famous for translating the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate)</note> also writes in the **Epistle he wrote to Laeta concerning the education of her daughter: Small things are not to be despised, for without them great things cannot endure.** <note>original Latin: "Hieron. in Epist. quam de institutione Filiæ scripsit ad Letam: Non sunt contemnenda quasi parva, sine quibus magna consistere non possunt."</note>

This is not to say that **Theology** must regulate and guide itself according to **Logic**, as **Piscator** perhaps teaches in his response to Buscher, chapter 14; or as if **Theology** should be explained and proven through the art of Reason, as **Ursinus** suggests in Volume 2 of his *Exposition of the Catechism*, page 552; also **Georg Lupichius** against Selnecker, page 7; **Beumler** in his *Hundred Synopses*; **Heilbrunner**, page 177; and **Boquinus** in his *Canons*, cent. 3, pages 34–35. Quintilian was a famous Roman educator whose work on the training of an orator was rediscovered and highly valued during the Reformation.</note>

Likewise, we also judge concerning Logic, **that it is the pinnacle of all disciplines,** <note>original Latin: "quod sit culmen omnium disciplinarum"</note> as Plato says in Book 2 of *The Republic*, and Francesco Patrizzi in Volume 3 of his *Peripatetic Discussions*, Book 4, page 313. For if anyone wishes to accomplish anything fruitful in Theology—not to mention the other faculties—and practice the <term>rightly dividing</term> <note>original Greek: ὀρθοτομεῖν (orthotomein). St. Paul uses this word to describe the duty of a teacher to cut a straight path through the Word of Truth without deviating into error.</note> of which Paul speaks in 2 Timothy 2, and rightly divide the word of truth, it is necessary that he be a logician. Not indeed as if Theology must regulate and direct itself according to Logic, as Johannes Piscator perhaps teaches in his refutation of Buscher, chapter 14; or as if Theology should be explained and evaluated out of the art of reason, as Ursinus suggests in Volume 2 of his *Explanations of the Catechism*, page 552; likewise Georg Lupich against Selnecker, page 7; Beumler in his *Synoptic Century*, Hailbrunner page 177; and Boquin in his *Canons*, canon 3, pages 34–35. Rather, it is only a helpful means, so that one can pursue theological studies more readily and effectively; otherwise it is as Chrysostom says in his 5th Homily on 1 Corinthians: **[To measure] divine matters by philosophy...** <note>original Latin: "Res divinas ex Philosophia"</note>

### Q. 12. Is it, however, advisable to read the books of the pagans?

Although the Enthusiasts and Anabaptists <note>The "Enthusiasts" (*Enthusiasten*) and "Anabaptists" (*Widerteuffer*) were radical Reformation-era groups who often rejected formal education and secular "arts" in favor of direct spiritual revelation.</note> not only cast out and reject the languages and the arts, but also the writings and books of the pagans, we nevertheless have examples and proof of this in the Scriptures: that we should test everything and keep only that which is good (1 Thessalonians 5). Just as the bees fly here and there, landing now on this herb and then on another, yet they do not carry the flowers away with them, but only suck the honey from them—**they do not take the flowers, but only suck out as much as is sufficient for making honey, leaving the rest behind** <note>original Latin: *non flores auferunt, sed tantum exfugunt, quantum ad mellificium sufficit, cetera relinquunt*</note>.

So too a Christian, **who is engaged in Christian literature** <note>original Latin: *qui in literaturâ Christianâ versatur*</note>, has good cause, power, and right to fly about like a spiritual little bee. He may not only pluck the beautiful herbs upon the green meadows of God's Word and suck the noble juice of faith from the flowers of Evangelical comfort, but he may also—next to the Scriptures—alight upon the philosophers' pleasure garden <note>original German: *Philosophen Lustgarten*</note>. He may visit their little flowers, and yet not take them away with him, but only test and practice them, speaking out the best parts and leaving the harmful weeds standing.

For of this we have the example of Moses, who was taught **in all the wisdom of the Egyptians** <note>original Greek: *ἐν πάσῃ σοφίᾳ Αἰγυπτίων*, from Acts 7:22</note>. We also read of Daniel, that he studied in the school of the Chaldeans and learned the Chaldean script and language; and God gave to him and his brothers skill and understanding in all kinds of writing and wisdom. # Heldenbuch
<note>The *Heldenbuch* or "Book of Heroes" is a title typically associated with collections of German epic poetry, but here it serves as a header for a discourse on the value of classical and secular learning.</note>

...writings in which to practice, especially because they are not nearly as offensive and harmful to the soul as the errors and books of heretics. For through false teaching, the human soul is stained and defiled when one agrees with it; this does not merely concern temporal and perishable things, but the **Eternal and imperishable Good**. Philosophical and heathen books, however, are so useful and profitable that whoever studies them diligently becomes a world-wise person. Therefore, it is rightly said: *Philosophy is as much the perfection of the soul as medicine is that of the body* <note>original Latin: *Philosophia ita est animae perfectio, ut corporis medicina.* Citations: Simplicius in his introduction to the *Physics*; Francesco Bonamico, book 1, *On Motion*, chapter 9, page 52; and Iacopo Mazzoni, section 8, chapter 5, page 281 and following.</note>. Therefore, one must read such books *with discernment* <note>original Latin: *cum judicio*</note>, so that one sucks out and keeps the good, and lets the evil remain.

Fifthly, the ancient **Church Fathers** <note>The influential theologians and scholars of the early Christian church.</note> likewise did not shy away from reading heathen and philosophical books, as we clearly see in the works of **Augustine**, particularly in his third letter *to Volusianus* <note>original Latin: *ad Volusianum Ep. 3.* St. Augustine (354–430 AD) was a pivotal figure in Western Christianity.</note>. For there he cites **Pherecydes, Pythagoras, Cicero, Virgil, Sallust**, and others, all of whom were heathen writers. Similarly, **Justin Martyr** <note>An early Christian apologist who sought to reconcile Greek philosophy with Christian faith.</note> composed a specific *Exhortation* <note>original Latin/Greek: *Parænesin*</note> *to the Greeks or Gentiles*, in which he proves in great detail—using heathen books—*that the Christian religion is older than the Heathen one* <note>original Latin: *quod Christiana religio sit vetustior Ethnicâ*</note>. **Clement of Alexandria** wrote an *Exhortation* <note>original Greek: *προτρεπτικὸν* (Protreptikos)</note> to the Gentiles; **Origen** responded in eight books to the slanders of the philosopher **Celsus**, who had most petulantly traduced the Christian religion. **Socrates** <note>Socrates Scholasticus (c. 380–439 AD), a historian of the early church.</note>, in the third book of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 10, repeats certain arguments—both **refutative** <note>original Greek: *ἀνασκευαστικὰ* (anaskeuastika), arguments meant to dismantle an opposing view.</note> and **constructive** <note>original Greek: *κατασκευαστικὰ* (kataskeuastika), arguments meant to build up or support a position.</note>—concerning the study of philosophy, to which I also refer the reader.

### Of the Rose Garden.

From all this, it can be honestly and rightfully seen and understood that these **haters and mockers of languages and arts** <note>original Latin: *osores & risores linguarum & artium*</note>, who nevertheless want to be masters of the Scripture, do not themselves understand what they say or what they assert, as Paul speaks in 1 Timothy 1. They are people of corrupted minds, unfit for the faith; but they will not proceed for long, for their folly will be manifest to everyone (2 Timothy 3:9). For how should one study the languages and liberal arts—**Grammar, Logic, and Rhetoric** <note>original: *Grammaticam, Dialecticam & Rhetoricam*. These three subjects formed the "Trivium," the foundation of a classical education.</note>? Why should one not read pagan books, since the Apostles themselves and the ancient Church Fathers did so? As **Jerome** <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the Church Father famous for translating the Bible into Latin.</note> also writes in his commentary on Daniel, chapter 1 (as found in Canon 11, Distinction 37): "Those who refuse to eat from the King's table and drink his wine lest they be defiled—surely, if they knew the very wisdom and doctrine of the **Babylonians** <note>The text refers to the biblical story of Daniel, who was educated in the Babylonian court but refused the king's food to remain ritually pure.</note> were a sin, they would never have agreed to learn what was unlawful. However, they learn not to follow it, but to judge and refute it. Just as someone wishing to write against mathematicians would be a laughingstock if they were ignorant of mathematics, or someone disputing against philosophers if they were ignorant of the philosophers' dogmas." Compare Canon 3, 9, 10, and 13, Distinction 37 <note>These citations refer to the *Decretum Gratiani*, a foundational collection of Canon Law used in the Church.</note>.

Aquil.* The Lex Aquilia was a Roman law providing compensation for damage to property, including injury to slaves.</note> *For he is held liable under the Aquilian Law who chastises a servant too harshly; and under the Cornelian Law concerning assassins* <note>original Latin: *Corneliâ de sicariis*</note> *whoever kills by fraud; how much more so the one who too harshly rebukes and corrects a free man, whom he ought to have shaped with virtues and disciplines.* <note>Translator's note: The author here cites several legal scholars: Hugues Doneau (*Donell.*), Jean Bodin (*Bodin.*), and Willem Gaeddeus (*Gædd.*) to emphasize that education should be formative, not abusive.</note>

## Q 2. Is it, however, useful and beneficial to study Philosophy?

These "New Heavenly Prophets" <note>A derogatory label used by orthodox Lutherans for radical reformers like the Schwenkfeldians or Anabaptists who claimed direct revelation from the Holy Spirit.</note> teach and speak of <term>philosophy</term> <note>The study of logic, ethics, and nature, which formed the core of the university curriculum.</note> in a most disparaging way, and do not wish us to apply our minds to it or study it. Everyone at the universities is obsessed with pagan <term>philosophy</term> and studies <term>Aristotle</term> <note>The Greek philosopher whose works on logic and physics were the foundation of higher education.</note>. But Christ—in whom the whole fullness of the Godhead and all wisdom dwells—is rejected, and everything is turned upside down. From this, it is also divided—with respect to its goal and subject—into **theoretical** <note>original: "θεωρητικὴν" (theōrētikēn)</note> and **practical** <note>original: "πρακτικὴν" (praktikēn)</note>, as Aristotle writes in the first book of the *Metaphysics*, chapter 2, and the first book of the *Topics*, chapter 9. **Theoretical philosophy** perfects the intellect and finds its rest in contemplation <note>original: "θεωρίᾳ" (theōria)</note> or knowledge. **Practical philosophy** rules the appetite <note>The "appetite" here refers to human desires and the will.</note> and finds its rest in deed <note>original: "πράξει" (praxei)</note> or action. **Theoretical philosophy** contemplates all things that exist <note>original: "ὄντα" (onta)</note>, as well as their principles and attributes, for the sake of science and truth. **Practical philosophy** deals with human actions and directs them toward the reins of right reason and the norm of honesty.

Who will now say that Philosophy is reprehensible and unnecessary, when it helps our corrupted Nature <note>A reference to the theological concept that human nature was "corrupted" by the Fall of Man; philosophy is seen here as a tool to help restore human reason.</note> back to the right path and teaches us both <term>to know</term> <note>original: "scire"</note> and <term>to act</term> <note>original: "agere"</note>—that we may understand something and also be able to perform it usefully? Is it not rather the case that without the knowledge of Philosophy, we cannot understand anything thoroughly, even in natural things, much less can we achieve anything fruitful in other faculties? But when we are experienced in Philosophy, we can obtain knowledge of many things from the **Great Book of Nature and Creation**, and understand their powers and natures <note>original: "earumque scire & intelligere vires & naturas"</note>. From this, Paul also argues in Romans 1: "For what is known of God is manifest to them, for God has manifested it to them. Thus, God's invisible essence—that is, His eternal power and divinity—is seen, if one takes notice of it in His works, namely in the creation of the world. While they held themselves to be wise, they became fools, and they changed the glory of the incorruptible God into an image like corruptible man, and birds, and four-footed and creeping animals."

II. *Every science has its own principles,* <note>original Latin: "Omnis scientia habet sua principia"</note> as **Aristotle** notes in *Posterior Analytics*, book 1, chapter 10, text 76; **Zabarella** <note>Giacomo Zabarella (1533–1589), a leading Aristotelian philosopher at the University of Padua.</note> in *On the Threefold Precognition*, book 1, chapter 1; and the Scholastics in book 1... beyond which it is not permitted to ascend. **Trelcatius** <note>Lucas Trelcatius (1542–1602), a Dutch Reformed theologian.</note>, *Common Places*, book 1, page 14. But Theology is a science, as **Trelcatius** says in his *Common Places*, page 17. **Danaeus** <note>Lambert Daneau (c. 1530–1595), a prominent French Reformed theologian.</note>, *Commentary on the Enchiridion of Augustine*, chapter 2, *whose authority alone suffices for maintaining piety and refuting errors,* <note>original Latin: "cujus autoritas sola ad tuendam pietatem & refutandos errores sufficit"</note> **Basil the Great**, Epistle 80, page 334 of the Greek edition from the year 1551; and **Augustine**, *On the Unity of the Church*, chapter 3. Therefore, *it is not permitted to ascend above the principles of Theology.* <note>original Latin: "Ergo supra principia Theologiæ non licet ascendere."</note>

III. *All principles must be homogeneous* <note>original Greek: ὁμογενῆ (homogenē), meaning "of the same kind" or "related"</note> *with their subjects,* as **Aristotle** says in *Posterior Analytics*, book 1, chapter 7. However, the principles or premises <note>original Greek: λήμματα (lēmmata), meaning "assumptions" or "propositions" used in an argument</note> of Philosophy are entirely heterogeneous <note>original Greek: ἑτερογενῆ (heterogenē), meaning "of a different kind"</note> from the proper premises <note>original Greek: λήμμασι (lēmmasi)</note> of Theology <note>original Greek: οἰκείοις (oikeiois), meaning "suitable" or "belonging to its own nature"</note>.

IV. If the Articles of Faith are measured and explained according to Reason and Philosophy, they are no longer articles of faith, but of sight <note>meaning "articles of observation"; the author is contrasting faith (belief in the unseen) with sight (rational or empirical proof)</note>, as **Danaeus** himself confesses in his *Commentary on the Enchiridion of Augustine*, chapter 4, page 15. *For there is no logical demonstration for the articles of faith,* <note>original Latin: "nullas enim est demonstratio articulorum fidei"</note> as **Thomas Aquinas** says, part 1, question 46, article 2. Therefore, we should simply remain by God’s Word, and take off the "shoes of **Reason**"—as Moses and Joshua did—whenever we approach God (Exodus 3, Joshua 5). *We should not resist God, even if what is said seems absurd to our senses and our blindness; for we cannot be deceived by the words of the Lord, whereas our senses are most easily deceived,* <note>original Latin: "nec repugnemus Deo, licet sensui & caecitati nostrae absurdum esse videatur, quod dicitur, nam verbis Jehovae defrauderinon possumus, sensus autem noster deceptui facillimus est"</note> as **Chrysostom** <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), an influential early Church Father known for his powerful preaching and biblical commentaries.</note> writes in Homily 83 on the 26th chapter of Matthew. Just as **Scaliger** <note>Julius Caesar Scaliger (1484–1558), a celebrated Italian scholar who was a dominant figure in Renaissance science and literary theory.</note> teaches in *Exercise 307, folio 29*: *There are many things in the sublunary world* <term>sublunary world</term><note>The physical realm of Earth "under the moon," which in traditional science was considered a place of constant change and imperfection compared to the heavens.</note> *which cannot be investigated by the sharp edge of the human mind; for it is a part of human wisdom to be willing to remain ignorant of certain things with a calm mind. And in even the most obvious things, our intellect is sometimes blind,* <note>original Latin: "multa sunt in orbe sublunari quae acie humanae mentis pervestigari nequeunt, humanae enim sapientiae est quaedam aequo animo nescire velle: Et in manifestissimis aliquando intellectus noster caecutit"</note> as **Aristotle** <note>The ancient Greek philosopher whose logic and metaphysics dominated European thought for centuries.</note> says in his *Metaphysics*, Book 2, chapter 1.

How then should we reach and comprehend the unfathomable mysteries of the **Articles of Faith**? For this reason **Luther** <note>Martin Luther (1483–1546), the primary figure of the Protestant Reformation.</note> admonishes us in the Jena Edition, Volume 6, folio 175: "Whoever wishes to travel safely should guard himself against everything where Reason and human thoughts attempt to master this Article [of faith]. Know that there is no counsel to withstand the Devil's deception except to cling to the naked, clear Word of Scripture. Think and speculate no further; instead, simply close your eyes and say: whatever Christ says, that shall and must be true, whether I or any other human can understand, comprehend, or know how it may be true. He knows well what He is, and what or how He should speak of Himself. Whoever does not do this must stumble, go astray, and fall; for it is simply not possible to comprehend even the least Article of Faith through human reason or senses." Thus, no person on earth—without God's Word—has ever been able to strike upon or grasp a right thought or certain knowledge of God, a fact that even the **Pagans** <note>original German: "Heyden"</note> themselves have had to testify.

### Book of Heroes
<warning>Dark stain/blot on the left margin near the beginning of the first paragraph.</warning>

Philosophers and theologians teach, both collectively and individually, that Philosophy is not opposed to Theology. Instead, it is subordinate and subservient to it, just like a master and servant, or a mistress and her maid. Indeed, Theology holds this title of honor and fame: **that she is the Mistress, while Philosophy is called the handmaid** <note>original Latin: *quod sit Domina, Philosophia autem dicitur pedissequa*. This was a standard medieval and Renaissance view of the sciences, where human reason serves divine truth.</note>. Just as the eyes of the servant look toward the hands of his master, and the eyes of the maid toward the hands of her mistress—as David says in Psalm 123—and they attend to them and are obedient, so too does Philosophy regulate and direct itself according to Theology, being helpful and attentive to it in all things.

By "Philosophy," however, we do not mean **every person’s every opinion, nor the pronouncements of foolish wisdom, but certain and firm knowledge** <note>original Latin: *non omnes omnium opiniones, nec effata insipientis sapientiæ, sed certas firmasq; notitias*</note>. To put it briefly, we mean Christian Philosophy, which stays within its own territory and circle: **Christian and sound philosophy, which contains itself within its own limits** <note>original Latin: *Philosophiam Christianam & sanam, quæ intra metas se continet*</note>. In this form, it is not against or contrary to the Word of God, **because the wisdom of God is not, and cannot be, contrary to itself** <note>original Latin: *quia sapientia Dei non est, nec potest esse sibi contraria*</note>. But when a person misuses their reason and tries to regulate <term>Holy Scripture</term> <note>original German: *H. Schrifft* (Heilige Schrift)</note> by it, or tries to out-think the articles of faith, that is a **fault of the person** <note>original Latin: *vitium personæ*</note>, which cannot be blamed upon or attributed to Philosophy itself.

Furthermore, the **term "contraries"** <note>original Latin: *vocabulum contrariorum*</note> is used in two ways. First: **generally, for things that are opposite** <note>original Latin: *generatim pro oppositis*; citing Aristotle’s *Metaphysics*, Book 10, Chapter 4</note>. Second: **specifically, for immediate opposites that fall under the same immediate category** <note>original Latin: *Speciatim pro oppositis immediatis, quæ sunt sub eodem genere proximo*; citing the scholar Julius Caesar Scaliger, *Exercitationes* 9</note>. In the **first way** <note>original Latin: *priori modo*</note>, we readily admit that there is a contrariety between Theology and Philosophy, but not in the **second way** <note>original Latin: *posteriori modo*</note>. For Philosophy teaches nothing other than what is good and true; for which reason Taurellus <note>Nicolaus Taurellus (1547–1606), a physician and philosopher known as the "first German philosopher."</note> says in *On Eternal Things*, page 62, **that truth is the goal**...

<meta>This page continues the argument that human reason and divine revelation are complementary. Having previously defined "Christian Philosophy" as a disciplined pursuit of truth, the author now refutes the idea that early Church authorities completely rejected philosophy, specifically addressing the writings of Tertullian.</meta>

->From the Rose Garden. 71<-

In Philosophy, whatever is good and true is not inherently opposed to another; **for every good accords with good, and every truth with truth.** <note>original Latin: *omne enim bonum bono, & omne verum vero consonat.*</note> (Aristotle, *Prior Analytics*, Book 1; Augustine, chapter 32; and Aristotle, *Nicomachean Ethics*, Book 3, chapter 9). Thus, no art or science can be the contrary of another, **nor does an associated field in use oppose its own subject of focus; neither are the Philosopher and the Theologian at odds.** <note>original Latin: *nec adjunctum occupatum contrariatur suo objecto occupato, nec Philosophus & Theologus sunt contrarii.*</note>

However, someone might object that Philosophy was rejected and discarded by Tertullian <note>Tertullian (c. 155 – c. 220 AD) was an influential early Christian author known for his sharp critiques of Greek philosophy, famously asking, "What has Athens to do with Jerusalem?"</note>, since he calls philosophers the **"patriarchs of heretics"** <note>original Latin: *hæreticorum patriarchas*</note>. Therefore, it is unnecessary to respond to such objections <note>The author suggests the answer is so clear that the objection holds little weight.</note>: for he does not speak <term>simply or generally <note>original Greek: *ἁπλῶς* (haplos)</note></term> but <term>in a certain respect <note>original Greek: *πῆ* (pe)</note></term> and he rejects the **abuse** or misuse of it, and not the right benefit and use. He rejects **not Philosophy itself, but the perverse dispositions of philosophers** <note>original Latin: *non Philosophiam sed Philosophorum prava ingenia*</note>, specifically when they invent and fabricate peculiar opinions and errors. He indicates this specifically regarding Valentinus, Marcion, Hermogenes, and similar heretics <note>These were prominent 2nd-century teachers whose interpretations of Christianity were declared heretical by the early Church.</note>, who all misused logic and philosophy to maintain their heresy. **However, the vice of the person cannot be blamed on Philosophy.** <note>original Latin: *vitium autem personæ non potest imputari Philosophiæ*</note>

### Question 4: Is not everything that is natural also
### spiritual and divine at the same time? Or do the Kingdom of Nature

# Book of Heroes

However, the art of medicine is not such a poor and contemptible thing; rather, it concerns human health and well-being. Just as much as health is of great importance, so too is medicine. Therefore, Sirach Chapter 38 says: Honor the physician with due reverence, so that you may have him in time of need. For the **LORD** has created him, and medicine comes from the Most High, and kings honor him. The art of the physician exalts him and makes him great among princes and lords. The **LORD** lets medicine grow out of the earth, and a sensible person does not despise it. <note>This refers to the biblical book of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 38:1–8, a standard defense of the medical profession in the early modern period.</note>

On account of such high status and importance, the art of medicine is called by *Hippocrates, Aphorism 1*, a <term>wide-ranging art</term> <note>original: *τέχνη μακρὴ* (*technē makrē*), from the famous aphorism: "Life is short, the art is long."</note>. And by *Galen in the book 'That the Best Physician is also a Philosopher'*, it is called a difficult and high art—indeed, the greatest among all arts. This is so for three reasons: 1. because of the fleeting opportunity; 2. because of dangerous experience; 3. because of difficult judgment. <note>original: *1. propter occasionem præcipitem. 2. propter periculosam experientiam. 3. propter difficile judicium.* These are the conditions Hippocrates cited as making medicine difficult.</note> For a *physician* <note>original: *Medicus*</note> must know how a person can be maintained in health, or if they have lost it, how they may regain it. He must learn the patient's nature and character, and have knowledge of <term>natural things, things not natural, and things contrary to nature</term> <note>original: *rerum naturalium, non naturalium & rerum præter naturam*; these were the three categories of medical study in the Renaissance: the body's makeup, external influences like diet/environment, and diseases.</note>. He must know how to properly distinguish between water and air, food and drink, waking and sleeping. Yet even that is not enough; a *physician* must also simultaneously be a <term>dialectician</term> <note>original: *Dialecticus*; someone skilled in logic and formal reasoning.</note>, as *Galen* demands in his book *'The Best Physician is also a Philosopher'*, so that he knows how to distinguish between diseases and how to categorize the entire nature and character of the human body.

Now, although *medicine* is such a high and difficult art, *Weigel* <note>Valentin Weigel (1533–1588), a German mystic whose followers often criticized institutional learning and academic science.</note> nonetheless rejects it entirely without thought—at least as it is taught and learned in the *academies* <note>universities</note>—in his *Book of Disputations, letter E. ij.* For this reason alone, because it...

Furthermore, he says that they [traditional physicians] administer herbs along with the <term>impure body</term> <note>original: *corpore impuro*; in alchemical medicine, this refers to the raw, unrefined state of a plant containing both healing and toxic elements</note>, mixing good and bad together—though always more of the bad—because they know nothing of <term>separating the impure</term> <note>original: *de separando impuro*; the alchemical process of refining a substance to its pure essence</note>.

But *Weigel* <note>Valentin Weigel (1533–1588) was a mystical theologian whose followers often rejected academic medicine in favor of spiritual and alchemical insights.</note> is not the first to so deeply belittle the <term>Galenists</term> <note>Followers of the Greek physician Galen, whose system of the four humors dominated European medicine for over a millennium.</note>; rather, *Theophrastus Paracelsus* had dared to do so not long before, as he clearly writes in his *Treatise on Long Life, page 217*: <term>no account of the humors is to be held in medicine</term> <note>original: *humorum ratio nulla est in medicina habenda*</note>. Despite this, experience sufficiently demonstrates that diseases take their origin and beginning from the <term>humors</term> <note>original: *humoribus*</note>. For there are four fluids in the human body, according to which a person is either healthy or sick. This is shown and reported not only by *Hippocrates' "On Humors"* and *Galen's eighth book of "The Doctrines of Hippocrates"*, but also by many other <term>physicians</term> <note>original: *medici*</note>, such as *Jean Fernel in his treatise on fevers, chapter 1; Pieter van Foreest on urines, page 21; Salomon Alberti on scurvy, thesis 48; Levinus Lemnius on the hidden miracles of nature, book 2, chapter 1; Duncan Liddel's Epitome of Medicine, book 1, chapter 2; Cornelius Celsus, Johann Crato von Krafftheim, Leonhart Fuchs, Johannes Scholzius*, and countless others.

Indeed, a person is healthy when the <term>humors</term> <note>original: *humores*</note> or fluids manifest and prove themselves to be moderate in both their quality and their quantity. However, a person is sick when one of the fluids becomes too small or too great, or when it is separated from the others and flows to a foreign place. For into whichever limb they flow, they excite disease within it. From this it follows that it is necessary to restore what is lacking if one of the fluids is too low, or to remove it if there is too much. In this way, *Hippocrates* describes <term>medicine</term> <note>original: *medicin*</note> in *On Winds, Volume 1, page 247*, as being an <term>addition and subtraction</term> <note>original: *adpositio & ablatio*</note>.

Since **jurisprudence** <term>Jurisprudentia</term> <note>The study and theory of law</note> establishes and orders nothing except what is Christian, laudable, and honorable, it is certainly a reckless thought and undertaking that **Weigel** <note>Valentin Weigel (1533–1588), a German mystical theologian whose followers often viewed secular institutions with suspicion</note> wishes to abolish its proper use because of its abuse, and to condemn and banish the entire legal profession. ### Q. 7. Is it fitting for Christians to use pagan laws?

**Indeed**, Weigel wishes to reject jurisprudence in his *Book of Disputations, section E. ii.* for this very reason: because it is taken from the pagans and is taught as pagan. Similarly, in times past, **Carlstadt**, **Thomas Müntzer**, **Struthius**, and other such **Anabaptists** <term>Wiedertauffer</term> <note>Radical Reformers who rejected infant baptism and often sought to replace secular legal systems with biblical law</note> wanted to reintroduce the **Mosaic Policy** <term>Mosaische Policey</term> <note>The civil and judicial laws of the Old Testament</note> and discard the pagan laws. This was sufficiently testified by the lamentable experience of the **Peasants' War** <note>A massive socio-religious revolt in 1524–1525 across German-speaking lands</note> in the years 1524 and 1525. 

But the **Augsburg Confession** <note>The primary confession of faith for the Lutheran Church, presented in 1530</note>, Article 16, teaches us to the contrary: that Christians can certainly judge and settle matters according to the **Imperial Laws** <note>Roman civil laws as adopted by the Holy Roman Empire</note> without violating their **conscience** <term>conscientz</term>. For the judicial order of Moses was not established, and the **court laws** <term>forenses leges</term> were not given to him, to last forever. Rather, they were only for a specific time, which was determined and appointed by God (Galatians 3:19, 28; Colossians 2:11; Hebrews 9:10). Furthermore, the Lord God did not give such laws to the pagans, but only to the Israelite people, which is why in the **proclamation** <term>promulgation</term> this condition was added: "In your families and kindreds" <note>original Latin: *In familijs & cognationibus vestris*</note>. Bending the bow / Psalm 18. Whatever has its origin and beginning from God is very good, necessary, and wholesome. Therefore, it follows unassailably that the state of war is also neither reprehensible nor damnable.

However, someone might think: "Help, dear God! Should warfare be considered good? Yet so much evil happens because of it, as experience tells us; all kinds of unrest and disaster, destruction and devastation, misery and need, murder and theft, imprisonment and distress arise from it." Answer: It is true that much evil is mixed in with it, but that is only an abuse of warfare, or it consists of *vices of the soldiers which are not to be attributed to the military service: for the desire to harm,* as Augustine says against the Manichaeans, *the cruelty of revenge, an implacable mind, the ferocity of rebellion, the lust for power, and similar things; these are what are rightly blamed in war, and which are often also rightly punished, etc. For wars themselves are undertaken to be waged by good men.* <note>original: "vitia militum quae militiae non imputantur: nocendi enim cupiditas, ut ait August. cont. Manich. ulciscendi crudelitas, implacabilis animus, debellandi feritas, Libido dominandi, & si qua similia, hae sunt quae in bello jure culpantur, quae plerumque etiam jure puniuntur, &c. gerenda ipsa bella suscipiuntur à bonis." This quote from Saint Augustine (354–430 AD) is a foundational text for "Just War" theory, distinguishing the institution of the military from the personal sins of soldiers.</note> For that warfare is good in itself and ordained by God for the punishment of sins has not only already been touched upon, but the Prophet Isaiah also reports it in Chapter 1: If you will not obey and are disobedient, you shall be devoured by the sword.

Here it is now to be considered with diligence: when warfare is to be called "good" and pleasing to God. It must not be a wanton, unlawful coercion, nor a harmful and dangerous rebellion—as unfortunately now happens in the world, where lawful wars are seldom waged. Instead, it is mostly out of pride and luxury, out of strife and envy, because one person begrudges another what God has bestowed upon him. For such things God has no pleasure; they will also find it difficult to answer for it, those <term>war-throats</term> <note>original: "Kriegsgurgeln." A derogatory term for warmongers or mercenaries who are "hungry" for the profit and violence of war.</note> who, without necessity, so miserably sacrifice many hundreds, yes, even several thousand people upon the <term>butcher’s block</term>. <note>original: "Fleischbanck." Literally a meat-counter or shambles; a metaphor for a battlefield where men are slaughtered like livestock.</note> Rather, it belongs to the lawful...

<meta>This page continues the theological argument regarding the "Just War" doctrine, specifically defining the criteria for a "just cause" and "right intention," drawing on the authority of Church Fathers and biblical examples of kings.</meta>

<header>Book of Heroes</header>

Wars: *a just cause and a just intention of the combatants: moreover, the cause of a just war is, as Augustine says in Question 10 on Joshua, if things taken by injury are not returned, or if a city has neglected to correct what was shamefully committed.* <note>original: "caussa justa, & intentio bellantium justa: caussa autem justa belli est, ut ait August. q. 10. in Jos. si ablata per injuriam non reddantur, vel si civitas neglexerit corrigere id quod turpiter admissum est"</note> Thus also writes Isidore in Book 17, Chapter 1: *War is rightly undertaken either to recover property or to repel injuries.* <note>original: "Bellum recte suscipitur, vel de rebus repetundis, vel de promulgandis injurijs."</note>

In such a manner, David had a legitimate cause when the Philistine freebooters besieged the city of Keilah <note>referred to as "Kegila" in the text</note> and plundered everything they found outside the city; in just this way, God himself commanded that he should set out with his army <note>original: "Zeug," referring here to military equipment or a gathered force</note> and strike the Philistines (1 Samuel 23). Likewise, Joash, the King of Israel, to whom Amaziah, the King of Judah, offered an unnecessary conflict and would not desist; Joash was told to come and face him in person. Because Amaziah could not rest in his own skin <note>an idiom for being restless or looking for trouble: "auff heiler Haut nicht schlaffen möchte"</note>, he succeeded in what he strove for: his people were beaten, and Amaziah himself was captured by Joash. All his silver and gold were carried away, his children were taken as hostages, and Joash secured peace for him through war (2 Chronicles 25) <note>original: "2. Par. 25," referring to the Book of Paralipomenon, the traditional name for Chronicles</note>.

Now, if such legitimate causes are present, and to them is added *a just and legitimate intention of the combatants, so that good is promoted and the good are defended,* <note>original: "justa & legitima bellantium intentio, ut bonum promoveatur & boni defendantur"</note> then wars can indeed be conducted with a good conscience; *for to serve as a soldier is not a sin, but to serve as a soldier for the sake of plunder is a sin.* <note>original: "militare enim non est peccatum, sed propter praedam militare peccatum est"</note> Therefore, let everyone look well to what he begins and performs, and let him first and foremost—if necessity indeed requires war—be commanded by the fear of God. Let him begin it in the fear of the Lord with dear prayer, and call upon God for help. If he does this, then with the Lord he will be able to leap over walls and subdue his enemies. But if he relies on his own strength and power, and in such a manner fights not only against his external enemy but also against God himself, then the hand of the Lord will be against him, and he will [be conquered]... <meta>The page ends mid-sentence; the catchword "bezwung" suggests "bezwungen" (conquered or subdued).</meta>

## Question 13. Is it not right that different degrees are accepted at universities?

Not only the <term>Anabaptists</term> <note>original German: "Widerteuffer," a radical Reformation group that often rejected state and church hierarchies.</note>, but also Carlstadt, Zwingli, and Gualterus, and now recently Weigelius, have rashly rejected <term>academic degrees</term> <note>original Latin: "gradus Academicos"</note>, as is known from his pamphlets. For in his work *On Serenity, chapter 43* <note>original German: "von der Gelassenheit," a key text by Valentin Weigel on the mystical path of letting go of the self.</note>, he says: "What else does one seek in the high schools <note>The original German "hohen Schulen" refers to universities.</note> but honor? One becomes a **Master**, the other a **Doctor**, which Christ nonetheless forbade his disciples; and yet such Masters and Doctors want to be the ones who teach and maintain the Christian faith." And in *On University Studies, letter H. 2.* <note>original Latin: "de stud. univers. lit. H. ij."</note> he says: "The <term>star-spirit</term> <note>original German: "Sternegeist," referring to the sidereal or astral mind in Weigelian thought, which he believed provided human reason but not divine wisdom.</note> becomes a **Licentiate**, a **Baccalaureate**, a **Master**, and a **Doctor**, but the Holy Spirit knows no such **Rabbis** <note>original Latin: "Rabinos," used here pejoratively to refer to academic masters who claim authority over scripture.</note>, nor has He been with them, as their lives and writings sufficiently testify."

However, this is an ancient and commendable custom, by which many a young student is encouraged to show himself all the more diligent in the **studies** he has begun, so that he might one day attain such honor and dignity. For <note>original Latin: "quippe honor esto non cuivis, sed digno tantum tribuitur, ne sui numerositate vilescat"</note> **honor should not be given to everyone, but only to the worthy, lest it become cheap through its abundance.** Just as an earthly prize is set up for which many wrestle and run, yet no one attains it except the one who reaches the mark and goal: so it is also with **degrees**, which are proposed and presented to studying youth like a beautiful prize of honor; yet no one can **regularly** <note>original Latin: "ordinariè"</note> receive them fruitfully if he does not penetrate and attain the **proper goal of erudition** <note>original Latin: "justam eruditionis metam."</note>.

But such **degrees** were not in use or practice **before the publication of Gratian’s Decree and Lombard’s Sentences** <note>original Latin: "ante editum Gratiani decretum & Lombardi sententias." ### Question 13. Is it not right that various degrees are accepted at universities?

**IT** is not only the **Anabaptists** <note>original: "Widerteuffer," a radical Reformation group that often rejected state and church hierarchies.</note>, but also **Karlstadt**, **Zwingli**, and **Gualther**, and now once again **Weigel**, who have thoughtlessly rejected **academic degrees** <note>original Latin: "gradus Academicos"</note>, as is well known from their pamphlets. However, it is an ancient and laudable custom, by which many a young student is refreshed and encouraged to show himself all the more diligent in his commenced **studies**, so that he might one day pursue such honor and dignity. **Indeed, honor is not to be given to just anyone, but only to the worthy, lest it become cheapened by its commonness.** <note>original Latin: "quippe honor esto non cuivis, sed digno tantum tribuitur, ne sui numerositate vilescat."</note> Just as a worldly prize is set up, for which many strive and run, yet no one attains it except the one who reaches the goal: so it is also with **degrees**, which are proposed and presented to studying youth like a beautiful jewel of honor; yet no one can **ordinarily** receive them profitably unless he has truly reached and won the **finish line of learning**. <note>original Latin: "am eruditionis metam."</note>

The terms "lytae" and "prolytae" were ancient Greek titles for law students in their final years of study.</note>

### Q. 14. Is it also useful and necessary that one practices by
->disputing at academies?<-

Master "Clever-clogs" <note>German: *Klügling*, a mocking nickname used by the author to disparage Weigel’s perceived intellectual arrogance</note> Weigel shows himself once again contrary in this matter and will allow no disputing—perhaps because his untruth and error might not be brought to light through opposing writings. Indeed, he himself writes that one cannot attain the truth through disputing, and that natural disputing is as useful to his studies (in his "Enthusiastic Theology" <note>A term used by mainstream theologians to describe the "Enthusiasts" or radical reformers who prioritized personal spiritual revelation over scripture and formal logic</note>) as the Devil is to the Church (in the preface to his book on disputation).

Initially, however, it is worth thinking and considering that through disputing we do not mix one thing into another—**Logic into Theology**. Whence Jerome <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century scholar known for the Vulgate Bible translation</note> rightly says and laments concerning such abuse: "*Lord, deliver us from dialectics*" <note>original Latin: *à Dialectica libera nos Domine*</note>. Nor should we understand by this those dangerous and unnecessary quarrels of which Paul speaks in 1 Timothy 6:3: "If anyone teaches otherwise and does not stay with the wholesome words of our Lord Jesus Christ, and with the doctrine of godliness, he is darkened and knows nothing, but is sick with questions and word-wars, from which arise envy, strife, blasphemy, evil suspicions, and school-wrangling by such men who have ruined minds and are robbed of the truth, who think that godliness is a business; withdraw yourself from such." Rather, we call it "disputing" in the proper sense when two people confer with one another through proposition and counter-proposition, through writing and counter-writing, so that the truth may be searched out and brought publicly to light: "**For truth is situated in a very deep well, blocked by many difficulties and surrounded by the most complex [obstacles...]**" <note>original Latin: *veritas enim in puteo sita est profundissimo, multis praeclusa difficultatibus, ac perplexissimis septa*</note>

...labyrinths; and whoever wishes to inquire into and explore such a deep abyss of truth must certainly apply no small amount of sweat and diligence, but must constantly practice and test himself **by debating, reading, and meditating** <note>original Latin: *disputando legendo & meditando*</note>. **For just as fire is drawn out by the striking of stones together, so too is the truth drawn out of debates** <note>original Latin: *sicut enim lapidis collisione ignis, ita ex disceptationibus elicitur veritas*</note>, as Scaliger <note>Julius Caesar Scaliger (1484–1558), a renowned Italian scholar known for his works on grammar and philosophy</note> notes in his 308th Exercise.

That such **debating** <note>original: *disputiren*</note> and proper **conferring** <note>original: *conferiren*</note> is useful and necessary appears from the following reasons:

**I.** That which gives cause for diligent **study** <note>original: *studiren*</note> should rightly be loved and praised; debating gives such cause; **therefore** <note>original Latin: *Ergo*</note>, it must not be rejected, but rather loved and praised. 

**II.** It also brings benefit to languages and arts, in speaking and answering, so that one reads through the **authors** <note>original: *autores*</note> all the more diligently and thus becomes experienced and eloquent. 

**III.** Truth is explored through it, as Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational theologian of Western Christianity</note> also says in the first book of his questions on Genesis: **"It is not debate that is acquired by truth, but truth that is acquired by debate"** <note>original Latin: *non disputatio veritate, sed veritas disputatione acquiritur*</note>.

**IV.** The **intellect** <note>original Latin: *ingenium*</note> and human understanding are also greatly **sharpened** <note>original: *acuirt*</note> thereby, as Augustine writes once again in his *Handbook to Laurentius* <note>original Latin: *Enchiridion ad Laurentium*</note>, chapter 59: **"When such things are sought after, and each person conjectures as he is able, the intellects are not uselessly exercised, provided that a moderate discussion is applied and the error of those who think they know what they do not know is absent."**

**V.** The Apostle **Paul** also desires that teachers should hold fast to the Word which is certain and able to teach, so that they might be powerful enough to exhort through sound doctrine and to convict those who contradict (Titus 1:9). Now, if teachers are to be **refutative** <note>original Greek: *ἐλεγχτικοὶ* (elenchtikoi), meaning capable of proving an opponent wrong through evidence</note> and practice **debating**, then surely **debating** and **refuting** will bring more benefit to the Church than the Devil does—contrary to the blasphemous way Weigel <note>Valentin Weigel (1533–1588), a critic of formal church structures and academic theology</note> speaks. For the Devil brings only harm and destruction, but debating thwarts untruth, refutes error, strengthens faith, preserves the Word in pure understanding, and advances man toward all that is good.

**VI.** Thus the Apostle **Paul** warns that one should [test] everything...

# Of the Rose Garden.

But if we look at God’s Word and take experience as our counsel, we must judge to the contrary: that we here *in the land of imperfection and forgetfulness* <note>original: *in terra imperfectionis & oblivionis*</note> cannot learn everything perfectly, nor know and experience the future before it happens. Since St. Paul himself says in 1 Corinthians 13: *we know in part, and we prophesy in part* <note>original: *ἐκ μέρους γινώσκομεν, καὶ ἐκ μέρους προφητεύομεν*</note>; our knowledge is patchwork and our prophesying is patchwork. And GOD the LORD speaks through the prophet Isaiah, Chapter 41: Let them approach and announce to us what is to come: Announce to us and prophesy something beforehand, let us pay attention to it in our hearts, and note how it shall happen afterward: Or let us at least hear what is future: Announce to us what will come hereafter, so that we may know that you are gods. Since our knowledge is now piece by piece and patchwork, and God alone knows what is to happen in the future—which he has reserved for his own power, *Acts 1*—thus we say rightly with the prophet Isaiah, Chapter 41:24: You (<term>Chiliasts</term> <note>A term for Millenarians who believed in a literal 1,000-year earthly reign of Christ, often claiming special revelation about the timing of the end times.</note>) are of nothing, and your work is also of nothing, and choosing you is an abomination.

For what man knows God’s counsel? Or who can think what God wills? The thoughts of mortal men are uncertain, and our designs are dangerous. For the mortal body burdens the soul, and the earthly tent weighs down the distracted mind. We barely grasp that which is on earth, and we find with difficulty what is at hand: Who then will investigate what is in heaven? Who will know your counsel? Unless you give wisdom and send your Holy Spirit from on high, so that the deeds on earth become right, and men learn what pleases you, and are saved through wisdom, *Wisdom of Solomon 9, Isaiah 40* <note>original: *Sap. 9. Es. 40.*; The author cites the Book of Wisdom (Sapientia), which emphasizes that divine mysteries are inaccessible without God's gift of the Spirit.</note>. Our understanding is far too narrow, and God’s mysteries are much too high, so that we cannot grasp them, as David also says in *Psalm 139*: Such knowledge is too wonderful for me—
